q: Bangladesh's national fruit is the ___.
why: Mango gets the poetry and the summer headlines, but kathal gets the title. It is enormous, it smells like a decision, and every part of it gets eaten — seeds roasted, unripe flesh cooked as a vegetable.

q: Bangladesh's national flower is the ___.
why: Shapla grows wild in the flooded fields and ponds that cover much of the country for half the year. It is on the coat of arms, and children still string the stems into necklaces.

q: Bangladesh's national bird is the ___.
why: The doel is small, black-and-white, and startlingly loud for its size. It is on the coins, and Dhaka University's Doel Chattar roundabout is named after it.

q: Bangladesh's national fish is the ___.
why: Ilish is roughly an eighth of the country's fish catch and the centre of an argument that never ends: Padma or Meghna, fried or shorshe. Chandpur calls itself the Ilish capital and nobody has successfully disputed it.

q: Bangladesh's national animal is the ___.
why: It lives in the Sundarbans, and it is why the national cricket team are the Tigers. Counting them is genuinely difficult — the mangrove is tidal, trackless and mostly water.

q: Bangladesh's national tree is the ___ tree.
why: The fruit lost the national title to kathal, but the tree took it instead — a compromise nobody planned. Chapainawabganj and Rajshahi run on mango season the way other places run on harvest.

q: The Sundarbans is generally said to be named after the ___ tree.
why: Sundari is the dominant hardwood of the forest, and the usual reading of the name is 'sundari forest' rather than the tempting 'beautiful forest' — though Bengali being what it is, both meanings sit in the word at once.

q: Bangladesh's only coral island is ___.
why: Locally it is Narikel Jinjira — coconut island. It sits at the far southern tip near the Myanmar coast, and its reef is fragile enough that visitor numbers are now capped.

q: Bangladesh's famously long unbroken sea beach is at ___.
why: Around 120 km of it, which is regularly claimed as the longest natural sea beach in the world. It is named after Hiram Cox, an East India Company officer — one of the more durable pieces of colonial naming left on the map.

q: The town known as Bangladesh's tea capital, home of the seven-layer tea, is ___.
why: Surrounded by tea estates in Moulvibazar district. The seven-layer tea is a genuine local invention — density and sugar content keep the layers from mixing, and the recipe is a closely held secret.

q: The National Parliament building in Dhaka was designed by the architect ___.
why: Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban took over twenty years to build and is widely counted among the great buildings of the twentieth century. Muzharul Islam was offered it first and passed it to Kahn — an act of architectural generosity with few equals.

q: Dhaka's riverside 'Pink Palace' is properly called ___.
why: The residence of the Nawabs of Dhaka on the bank of the Buriganga. The pink is the point — it is visible from the river long before anything else on that bank resolves.

q: The oldest known urban archaeological site in Bangladesh is ___.
why: In Bogura, and the ancient city of Pundranagar. The earliest layers go back well over two thousand years, which puts a city on that spot long before most of the region's better-known capitals existed.

q: Bangladesh's Nobel Peace Prize was awarded for pioneering ___.
why: Muhammad Yunus and Grameen Bank shared the 2006 prize for small collateral-free loans, lent overwhelmingly to women. The model has been copied, praised and criticised across the world ever since.

q: The handwoven Dhaka muslin figured fabric on UNESCO's intangible heritage list is ___.
why: Woven on a handloom with no mechanical patterning at all — the motifs are added thread by thread by eye. UNESCO listed it in 2013, and a good sari can take months.

q: In 2023 UNESCO added Dhaka's ___ to its intangible cultural heritage list.
why: The hand-painted tin panels, the film stars, the tigers, the impossible landscapes. Listing it as heritage is slightly funny given the painters were never treated as artists — and entirely deserved.

q: The mystic wandering minstrels of Bengal, recognised by UNESCO, are the ___.
why: Lalon Shah is the towering figure. The songs sit deliberately outside organised religion, which is exactly why they have been loved and distrusted in roughly equal measure for two centuries.

q: The masked dawn procession that opens Pohela Boishakh in Dhaka is called ___.
why: Giant papier-mâché animals, students up all night building them, and a route through Dhaka University. UNESCO listed it in 2016.

q: UNESCO declared 21 February to be International ___ Day.
why: Proposed by Bangladesh and adopted in 1999, marking the date in 1952 when students died over the status of Bengali. It is the rare national commemoration that became a global one.

q: The words of Bangladesh's national anthem were written by ___.
why: 'Amar Sonar Bangla' was written in 1905. Tagore is the only person to have written the national anthem of two countries — India's is his as well.

q: Bangladesh's national poet is ___.
why: The Bidrohi Kobi — the rebel poet. He wrote furious anti-colonial verse and thousands of songs, and he is buried on the Dhaka University campus.

q: The Sixty Dome Mosque, a UNESCO World Heritage site, is at ___.
why: Shat Gombuj Mosque, part of the mosque city of Khalifatabad. The name is a nice piece of folk arithmetic — it does not have sixty domes, and counting them is a standard visitor argument.

q: The great Buddhist monastery ruin of Somapura Mahavihara is at ___.
why: Eighth century, in Naogaon, and one of the largest Buddhist monasteries south of the Himalayas. Its plan is thought to have influenced monastery architecture as far away as Southeast Asia.

q: The historic capital of Bengal near Dhaka, famous for muslin, is ___.
why: 'Golden hamlet'. Its abandoned Panam Nagar street of merchant houses is one of the strangest places in the country — a whole colonial-era high street left standing and empty.

q: Bangladesh's national game is ___.
why: Locally Ha-Du-Du. Cricket is what the country actually watches, which makes the official title a small ongoing joke — the national game and the national obsession are not the same sport.

q: The Bangladesh national cricket team is nicknamed the ___.
why: After the Royal Bengal tiger. The team's supporters bring actual tiger costumes to grounds, which has made the nickname unusually literal.

q: The Dhaka biryani made with raw marinated mutton and rice cooked together in a sealed pot is ___.
why: Kacchi means raw — the meat is not pre-cooked, so the pot has to be judged exactly. It is the default wedding food, and an opinion about the best kacchi in Dhaka is close to mandatory.

q: The dish traditionally eaten on Pohela Boishakh morning is ___ with fried hilsa.
why: Rice soaked in water overnight — historically what you ate because you were poor, now what you queue for on new year's morning. The irony is widely noted and cheerfully ignored.

q: The embroidered quilt made by stitching together old saris is called ___.
why: Nothing is wasted: worn cloth is layered and quilted, and the running stitch becomes the picture. Jasimuddin's poem 'Nakshi Kanthar Math' made it a national symbol.

q: Dried, salted and cured fish, beloved and divisive, is called ___.
why: Chittagong and the coastal districts are the strongholds. It is the one food most likely to get a diaspora household a complaint from the neighbours, and the one most likely to be worth it.

q: The three great rivers whose combined delta forms most of Bangladesh are the Padma, the Jamuna and the ___.
why: The Ganges arrives as the Padma, the Brahmaputra as the Jamuna, and the Meghna carries the combined flow to the sea — one of the largest discharges of fresh water on Earth.

q: The Sylheti language historically had its own script, called ___.
why: Used for centuries for religious and folk texts, largely displaced by Bengali script, and now the subject of a real revival. It has had its own Unicode block since 2005.

q: The largest Indigenous group of the Chittagong Hill Tracts is the ___.
why: The Hill Tracts are home to about a dozen Indigenous peoples with their own languages, and Chakma has its own script descended from the Burmese family. Biju, their new year festival, runs alongside Pohela Boishakh.

q: The sweet that made the town of Muktagacha famous is ___.
why: Bangladesh's sweets are fiercely regional: monda from Muktagacha, chomchom from Porabari, mishti doi from Bogura. Bringing the wrong town's sweet to a wedding is noticed.

q: The everyday Bangladeshi English term for a scheduled power cut is ___.
why: A piece of utility jargon that became ordinary speech. Whole childhoods are structured around it — homework by candle, the fan stopping, and the particular cheer of the whole neighbourhood when it comes back.

q: In Dhaka, a 'CNG' means a ___.
why: Named after the fuel, compressed natural gas, and now simply the name of the vehicle. Caged, green, metered in theory, and negotiated in practice.

q: The dish Bangladeshis famously crave the moment it starts raining is ___.
why: Rice and lentils cooked together, with beef or ilish or just a fried egg. The rain-khichuri connection is close to a national reflex and survives every kind of relocation.

q: The crisp hollow street snack filled with spiced potato and tamarind water is called ___ in Bangladesh.
why: Golgappa and pani puri are the same idea under other names elsewhere — and the differences in filling and sourness are real enough to start an argument at any diaspora gathering.

q: The cash that children collect from elders at Eid is called ___.
why: Crisp new notes, obtained from the bank specially. The rate is set by nothing but reputation, and the accounting done by cousins afterwards is merciless.

q: The turmeric ceremony held before a Bangladeshi wedding is the ___.
why: Literally 'turmeric on the body'. It has quietly become the most-photographed event of the whole wedding, and in the diaspora it is often the one night the entire extended family actually turns up.

q: The reception hosted by the groom's family after a Bangladeshi wedding is called ___.
why: Literally 'bride's rice' — the bride formally serving rice to her new household. In practice it is a very large lunch with a very long queue for the stage photo.

q: London's Banglatown, lined with curry houses and hung with green-and-red arches, is centred on ___.
why: The street has been a first stop for wave after wave of migrants — Huguenot, Jewish, then Bengali. The same building on the corner has been a chapel, a synagogue and a mosque.

q: The London borough with the largest Bangladeshi population is ___.
why: Bangladeshis are the largest single ethnic group in the borough, and it has elected Bangladeshi-origin councillors and mayors for decades. Canary Wharf's towers are in the same borough, which makes the inequality unusually visible.

q: The overwhelming majority of British Bangladeshis trace their origin to the ___ region.
why: It began with Sylheti lascars working the steamship engine rooms out of Kolkata, and chain migration did the rest. It is why Sylheti, not standard Bengali, is the community language of British Banglatown.

q: The first Bengalis to settle in Britain in numbers arrived as ___ on British ships.
why: Sylheti men crewed the boiler rooms of steamships out of Kolkata, and some stepped off in London and stayed. The community is older than most people assume — there were Bengali sailors in the East End in the nineteenth century.

q: The New York neighbourhood that is the centre of Bangladeshi life in the city is ___.
why: Seventy-Third Street and Thirty-Seventh Avenue, sari shops and mishti and a Bangladeshi bookshop. Kensington in Brooklyn is close behind, with its own stretch renamed Little Bangladesh.

q: Chicago's South Asian commercial strip, thick with Bangladeshi and Indian shops, is ___ Avenue.
why: Honorary street signs along it carry both Indian and Bangladeshi names, on the same road, a few blocks apart — a piece of civic diplomacy done entirely in signage.

q: The small Michigan city with a large Bangladeshi community and a Bangladeshi-American majority on its city council is ___.
why: Historically a Polish city entirely surrounded by Detroit, now one of the most immigrant-dense places in America. The stretch along Conant is known as Banglatown.

q: The dish a British Foreign Secretary once called 'a true British national dish' is ___.
why: Robin Cook, in a 2001 speech about multiculturalism. The dish barely exists in South Asia — it was invented for British tastes, in kitchens largely staffed by Sylhetis.

q: For decades, the large majority of Britain's 'Indian' restaurants were actually owned and run by ___.
why: Commonly put at around two-thirds to three-quarters of the trade. 'Indian' was a commercial decision, not a description — it was the word the customers already knew.

q: The first British MP of Bangladeshi origin, elected in 2010, was ___.
why: Elected for Bethnal Green and Bow — the Tower Hamlets seat, which makes the timing look less inevitable than it was: the community had been there for generations before it sent one of its own to Parliament.

q: In diaspora slang, 'ABCD' stands for American Born Confused ___.
why: Affectionate, insulting or self-applied depending entirely on who is saying it. The full joke continues through the alphabet — the rest is rarely remembered and never as good.

q: Across the diaspora, the weekend institution that teaches children Bengali is usually called ___.
why: Usually a rented hall, a volunteer teacher and children who would rather be anywhere else. It is also, quite often, the only reason the next generation can read a Bengali alphabet at all.

q: The largest number of Bangladeshi migrant workers abroad are in ___.
show: The Gulf (especially Saudi Arabia and the UAE)
why: The Western diaspora is the visible one — the restaurants, the MPs, the students. The far larger migration is to Gulf construction and domestic work, on contracts that rarely lead to settlement.

q: Europe's largest Bengali street festival, held each summer in Tower Hamlets, is the ___.
why: Bengali new year moved outdoors into an East London park, with a crowd that has run into the tens of thousands. The date drifts to fit the British summer, which is its own small act of adaptation.

q: The single most reliable way to cause offence entering a Bangladeshi home anywhere in the world is to keep your ___ on.
why: The pile by the door is the real front door. In colder countries this survives entirely intact, which is why every diaspora hallway has a shoe mountain and a visitor standing on one leg.

q: Any woman of your parents' generation, related to you or not, is addressed as ___.
why: Kinship terms do the work that names do elsewhere. Getting it wrong in either direction — too junior, too senior — is a small social injury that the whole room registers immediately.

q: In 2010 the city of Los Angeles officially designated a neighbourhood called Little ___.
why: A small stretch near Koreatown, and the designation was genuinely contested — the community had to campaign for the signs against a competing claim on the same blocks.

q: Manchester's 'Curry Mile' runs through the district of ___.
why: A half-mile of Wilmslow Road, neon-lit and mostly South Asian-run. It is the closest thing outside London to Brick Lane, and just as much a student landmark as a community one.

q: The 'Balti Triangle', named after a style of curry served in a pressed steel bowl, is in ___.
why: The balti was invented in Birmingham, not in South Asia — a British dish with a South Asian name, cooked in restaurants largely opened by Pakistani and Bangladeshi families.

q: The Tower Hamlets electoral ward covering Brick Lane is officially named Spitalfields and ___.
why: One of very few places where a diaspora community's own name for its neighbourhood was written into the official map. The street signs run in both English and Bengali.

q: Italy's largest Bangladeshi community is concentrated in ___.
why: Centred on Torpignattara, to the point that the neighbourhood is nicknamed Banglatown. Italy has one of the largest Bangladeshi populations in Europe after Britain.

q: Monica Ali's 2003 novel about a Bangladeshi woman in London's East End is called ___.
why: Booker-shortlisted, and it caused a genuine argument on the street it was named after — some residents felt it caricatured them. That fight is now part of the book's story.

q: The long collarless shirt a Bangladeshi man wears to Eid is called a ___.
why: Confusingly named after a region nowhere near Bengal, and everywhere else in South Asia the same garment is a kurta. Bought a size large so it survives the year.

q: In the diaspora, Eid prayers are commonly held in a park or a rented ___ because no mosque is big enough.
why: Eid prayer happens once, at one time, and the whole community turns up at once — so the building that fits it is a sports centre with the badminton lines still on the floor.

q: Outside the Gulf, the single largest destination for Bangladeshi migrant workers has been ___.
why: Plantations, factories and construction, on recruitment schemes that have been repeatedly suspended and restarted over allegations of exploitation. Singapore's shipyards are the other large Southeast Asian draw.

q: Anything mashed up with mustard oil, raw onion and green chilli becomes a ___.
why: Potato, aubergine, dried fish, coriander, even a single roasted chilli — bhorta is a technique rather than a recipe. It is the cheapest thing on the table and reliably the first bowl to be scraped out.

q: The Bengali five-spice mix, dropped into hot oil whole and never ground, is ___.
why: Fenugreek, nigella, cumin, black mustard and fennel in roughly equal parts. Keeping them whole is the entire point — the seeds pop at different moments, so the oil picks up five things instead of one.

q: The curved floor-mounted blade a cook squats over to gut a fish is a ___.
why: The blade is fixed and the food moves — you bring the fish to it with both hands. That is why it lives on the floor, and why nobody who learned on one ever fully trusts a chopping board.

q: Before the blender arrived, every spice paste in the house was ground on a ___.
why: A flat slab and a stone roller. Cooks insist a shil-ground mustard paste tastes different from a blended one and they are not imagining it — stone crushes where a blade cuts.

q: The foot-pedalled wooden husking beam that turns rice into flour for pitha is a ___.
why: One woman stands on the lever, another turns the rice in the hollow, and the thud carries across a village at dawn all through pitha season. Mills finished it off, and the flour is still said to be better.

q: The salted, spiced yoghurt drink poured out beside a plate of kacchi is ___.
why: Mint, mustard, black salt, green chilli and thinned yoghurt — engineered rather than invented, to cut through a plate of mutton and ghee rice. Sweet lassi at a wedding would be a category error.

q: The plank-and-tin roadside stall where tea is drunk standing up is a ___ shop.
why: Four planks, a kettle, a bench and a bank of biscuit jars. The tong is where cricket, politics and the neighbourhood's business get settled, and a cup costs less than the walk home.

q: Old Dhaka's dry, layered, saucer-sized bread, eaten with morning tea, is ___.
why: It keeps for days without going stale, which is the whole design — a bread built for a city rather than a kitchen. The name is attached to a Mughal-era love story that gets longer every time it is told.

q: Dhaka's yellow rice with small cubes of beef, cooked in mustard oil, is ___.
why: Mustard oil is the tell. Kacchi is ghee and ceremony; tehari is what an office lunch and a cricket match actually run on, and Old Dhaka will argue for an hour about which shop still does it properly.

q: Chittagong's beef, fried down for hours until the gravy is almost black, is ___.
why: No water goes in after the first hour — the colour comes from the meat's own juice reducing back onto it with fried onion and a heavy hand of spice. It is served with white rice and nothing that could distract.

q: The Chittagonian feast where a whole neighbourhood is fed beef and rice is a ___.
why: Anyone may walk in — no invitation, no list, no seating plan. It is held for a death, a birth, a good year or no reason at all, and the accounting is done in cattle rather than in guests.

q: The knobbly Sylheti citrus that goes into beef curry and is never eaten raw is ___.
why: It is mostly rind and bitterness, which is exactly the job — a few slices cut the fat of the beef. British Bangladeshi households bring it back frozen in suitcases and ration it like a currency.

q: In the south-west, meat curries take their heat from slices of a woody vine called ___.
why: You do not eat it — you chew a piece of stem, take the heat off it, and put it back on the plate. Khulna and Jashore treat a chui jhal beef as a regional examination, and outsiders always underestimate the dose.

q: The sharp fermented mustard sauce eaten with fried fish and bitter greens is ___.
why: It was once made ritually, on a fixed day, by women who had to keep the whole process clear of a long list of contaminants. Now it arrives in a bottle, and the bottle is still opened with a certain respect.

q: A large fish's head, broken up and cooked down with rice or lentils, becomes ___.
why: The head is the best part of the fish and it is given away on purpose — to the guest, the eldest, or the son-in-law currently being assessed. Wasting one sits somewhere near an insult.

q: The hard, sour fruit called 'elephant apple', cooked into dal and pickle, is ___.
why: What you eat is not really the fruit but the fibrous sepals around it, which is why it only ever turns up as a souring agent. The tree is a common sight and the fruit is a common theft.

q: The hard-shelled fruit smashed open and mashed with salt, chilli and mustard oil is ___.
why: It smells like something has gone wrong and tastes like a dare, and half the country would trade a mango for one. Sold already smashed at the roadside, because nobody wants to do that part at home.

q: Through the winter, sap tapped from date palms is boiled down into ___.
why: The pot goes up at dusk and comes down at dawn, because the sap starts fermenting as soon as the sun is on it. The entire winter sweet season runs on that overnight window.

q: The winter cake of steamed rice flour with gur and coconut hidden inside is ___.
why: Made in a cloth-lined bowl over a pot of boiling water, and sold on street corners the week the temperature finally drops. It has to be eaten standing there — cold, it is a different and much worse object.

q: The plain white rice pancake eaten with dried-fish bhorta or a puddle of gur is ___.
why: No sugar, no filling, cooked in a clay mould until one side is full of holes. It is the one pitha that goes savoury, and whether it belongs with shutki bhorta divides households permanently.

q: Grated coconut cooked down with gur and rolled into balls by hand makes ___.
why: Made in quantity before a festival and kept in a tin whose location everybody in the house knows. The gur version is dark and the sugar version is white, and people are loyal to one for life.

q: The town whose sweet yoghurt, set in an unglazed clay pot, is the national benchmark is ___.
why: The clay is doing real work: an unglazed pot pulls water out of the yoghurt as it sets, which is why the same doi in a plastic tub is a thinner, sadder thing.

q: The town that built its whole reputation on roshmalai is ___.
why: So many shops now claim to be the original that the dispute has outlived most of them. It travels badly, which has never once stopped anybody carrying a box of it onto a plane.

q: Natore's celebrated sweet, made of fresh chhana and barely cooked at all, is ___.
why: The name means 'raw ball', which undersells a sweet that is essentially warm curd and sugar and nothing else. Very little else on a mishti tray is that unforgiving — there is nothing to hide behind.

q: The dense, oblong sweet that made the village of Porabari famous is ___.
why: Porabari sits outside Tangail on the Dhaleshwari, and the story has always been that the river water made the difference. Everywhere sells chomchom now; the ones crusted with mawa are showing off.

q: The street bowl of boiled white peas, tamarind water and crumbled egg is ___.
why: Sold off a cart with a tin plate that gets rung with the spoon as advertising. The peas are cooked until they collapse, and the crushed fuchka shells over the top are not optional whatever anyone says.

q: In Bangladesh, the thick-crusted fried triangle filled with potato and peanuts is a ___.
why: Bangladeshis will insist a singara and a samosa are two different objects, and in a Dhaka bakery they are: the singara has the heavier pastry and the potato filling, the samosa is thinner and usually minced meat.

q: Puffed rice shaken up in a tin with mustard oil, chilli and chopped onion is ___.
why: The seller's tin is the instrument and the shaking is half the performance, and it comes to you in a cone folded out of yesterday's newspaper. Everything in it is cheap; nothing in it is optional.

q: The tiny, intensely aromatic rice cooked for polao and payesh is ___.
why: The grains are a fraction the length of basmati and the smell fills a house from two rooms away. It costs several times what everyday rice costs, which is why it comes out for guests and weddings only.

q: The northern district whose name is attached to Bangladesh's best-known litchi is ___.
why: Litchi season lasts about three weeks and the whole district reorganises around it, down to the trucks and the men who sleep under the trees guarding them. Buy late in the season and you are buying leftovers.

q: In late summer, the fruit whose thick orange pulp is squeezed out by hand for pitha is ___.
why: The pulp has to be pressed off the fibres through a sieve, which is filthy, patient work. The reward is taaler bora — fritters that exist for about a fortnight a year and then are gone.

q: A green coconut sold for its water, opened with three strokes of a machete, is a ___.
why: Once the water is gone you hand it back and the seller splits it so you can scrape the soft flesh out with a strip of the shell. That second half is what the regulars are actually there for.

q: The leaf folded around areca nut and lime and handed round after a heavy meal is ___.
why: Supari is the nut, chun is the lime and jorda is the tobacco — the leaf is only the wrapper, yet it gives the whole thing its name. A wedding with no paan tray at the door is remembered for it.

q: A formal Bengali meal is served in courses, and the first course is deliberately ___.
why: Bitter first — korola, neem leaves, something nobody would pick — then dal, vegetables, fish, meat, and sweet at the very end. Serving it out of order is the sort of thing an aunt brings up for years.

q: The rice-and-milk sweet a Bangladeshi mother cooks for a birthday is ___.
why: Milk cooked down for an hour with gur or sugar and, if the household is serious about it, chinigura rice. The cake is for the photographs; the payesh is the part that means the day counted.

q: The thin everyday lentil poured over rice in most Bangladeshi houses is ___.
why: Cooked thin enough to pour, tempered with garlic and dried chilli, and eaten with rice and nothing else on a thin week. Mug dal is for feasts; masoor is for Tuesday.

q: The oil whose raw sharpness is the smell of a Bangladeshi kitchen is ___.
why: It is pungent enough that most cuisines cook it out first; Bengali cooking often does the opposite and finishes a dish with a raw spoonful. A bhorta made with anything else is not a bhorta.

q: In Bangladesh, a cheap eatery serving rice and curry off a bench is normally called a ___.
why: Nobody sleeps there. A 'bhater hotel' is a plank bench, a rice pot and a row of curries under glass, and asking one for a room gets you a long, patient look.

q: The mild, faintly sweet chicken rice served at Dhaka wedding halls is ___.
why: It is the safe option — no mutton, no chilli, nothing that will defeat a child or a grandmother. Old Dhaka does a much heavier version with whole birds that has almost nothing to do with the wedding-hall one.

q: The bright orange sweet rice, studded with nuts, served after the meat at a feast is ___.
why: The same word names the tobacco tucked into a paan, which has confused every child ever handed one and offered the other. The colour has always been food dye and nobody pretends otherwise.

q: Mango pulp spread out on a tray and dried in the sun into dark sheets is ___.
why: A way of keeping a glut of mangoes long past the season, from before anyone owned a freezer. It is built up in layers over several days on a roof, defended from crows and children with about equal effort.

q: The Old Dhaka stew simmered all night and eaten with naan for breakfast is ___.
why: The name comes from the word for morning, and the whole idea is that it was cooking while you slept. The shops around Chawkbazar open before dawn and are sold out by the time the rest of the city eats.

q: Dhaka's pale mutton curry, thin with yoghurt and whole green chillies, is ___.
why: White, not brown — no browned onion and no turmeric, which is most of what makes it strange to anyone expecting a curry. It is court cooking that stayed on in Dhaka long after the court had gone.

q: The floral water flicked over polao and rezala at the last possible moment is ___.
why: Distilled from screwpine flowers and strong enough that one spoonful too many turns dinner into soap. A good half of a Dhaka biryani's smell arrives in the room before the dish does, because of it.

q: The Bengali spice seed whose name is also the Bengali word for 'cook' is ___.
why: It looks like celery seed, smells like nothing else on the shelf, and is one of the few spices with no honest substitute — which is why kitchens abroad hoard it and count what is left.

q: The fruit Bangladeshis claim makes your mouth water at the mere mention of it is ___.
why: Sold outside every school gate mashed with salt and chilli, and blamed for everything from ruined teeth to thinned blood by people who go on eating it regardless.

q: The Dhaka-born engineer who made Chicago's Sears Tower structurally possible was ___.
why: His 'bundled tube' idea let a tower carry its wind load on its skin instead of its frame, which is the reason tall buildings stopped being solid and started being affordable. He died in 1982 and is still taught in first-year structures courses.

q: Unlike Britain's Bangladeshi community, America's is largely not from ___.
why: Britain's community grew out of one district's ship-going networks. America's came later, through students, professionals and the visa lottery, and is drawn from the whole country — which is why a New York Bengali and a London Bengali often cannot place each other's accent.

q: The American immigration programme Bangladeshis simply called 'the lottery' is the ___ Visa.
why: For years it was the single widest door into America, and form-filling shops opened across Dhaka to handle the paperwork. Bangladesh was eventually dropped from the programme, having sent too many people through it to still count as under-represented.

q: The religious holiday New York City's schools added to their calendar in 2015, closing twice a year for it, is ___.
why: Both Eids, won after years of campaigning by a coalition in which Bangladeshi parents in Kensington and Jackson Heights were central. The practical effect is that no child has to choose between Eid prayers and an attendance mark.

q: Brooklyn's Bangladeshi centre, thick with Bengali groceries around Church Avenue, is ___.
why: Locals call it Little Bangladesh, which briefly confuses anyone who knows the Kensington in London. It has become the second pole of Bangladeshi New York, with Queens the first and a long subway ride between them.

q: In Jackson Heights, the Bangladeshi shops and restaurants cluster along ___ Street.
why: One block over, 74th Street is the Indian gold-and-sari strip. 73rd is where the Bengali sweet shops, phone-card sellers and immigration consultants are. The line is invisible to outsiders and non-negotiable to everyone else.

q: The Bronx neighbourhood that filled with Bangladeshi families and Bengali groceries is ___.
why: A planned housing development from the 1940s — lifts, lawns, and cheap by New York standards — which is exactly why families priced out of Queens started moving north into it.

q: Queens' other Bangladeshi high street runs along Hillside Avenue through ___.
why: Jackson Heights gets the photographs, but Hillside Avenue is where a good deal of the actual living happens — mosques, halal butchers, driving schools, and the sort of restaurant with no English anywhere on the menu.

q: Priced out of New York City, thousands of Bangladeshi families moved upstate to buy houses in ___.
why: A city with a surplus of empty houses met a community that badly wanted to own one. Buffalo's West Side filled with families who had spent a decade in a Queens basement, and the drive back for weddings is about seven hours.

q: The Bangladeshi district straddling the border of Detroit and Hamtramck is called ___.
why: One of the few places where a city line runs straight through a community's shopping street — half the groceries pay Detroit's taxes and half pay Hamtramck's, and everybody shops on both sides without noticing.

q: Banglatown's spine, lined with Bangladeshi groceries and sweet shops, is ___ Avenue.
why: Joseph Campau, one street across, is the old Polish main street; Conant is the Bangladeshi one. The two run parallel and roughly forty years apart.

q: Before Bangladeshis and Yemenis arrived, the Michigan city of Hamtramck was famously a ___ town.
why: The Dodge plant pulled in Polish workers by the tens of thousands and the city stayed Polish for most of a century — street names, churches, paczki bakeries and all. The bakeries are still there; the congregation changed.

q: Los Angeles carved its Little Bangladesh out of the edge of ___.
why: The community is small — a few blocks near Third Street — and the designation was fought hard precisely because it took territory from a far larger neighbour. Los Angeles hands out neighbourhood names by council vote, and this one went to a vote.

q: Houston's South Asian high street, full of Bangladeshi groceries and sari shops, is ___.
why: The stretch is officially the Mahatma Gandhi District — a name covering Bangladeshi, Pakistani and Indian businesses standing shoulder to shoulder and selling largely the same things to largely the same customers.

q: Vivek Bald's history of America's forgotten early Bengali settlers is called Bengali ___.
why: It pieced together men who arrived decades before the visa lottery, married into Black and Puerto Rican families, and then disappeared from the community's account of itself. Their descendants are still in the city.

q: In the 1890s Bengali pedlars sold embroidered silks to holidaymakers on the boardwalk at ___.
why: They were selling 'Oriental goods' to Americans who wanted the East without leaving New Jersey — and they were doing it a full century before anyone used the phrase Bangladeshi diaspora.

q: Bengali seamen who settled in mid-century Harlem most often married African American and ___ women.
why: They lived where they were permitted to live, which was Harlem, and married the neighbours. Their children grew up with Bengali cooking, Spanish, English, and no Bangladesh to visit.

q: The southern city where Bengali pedlars settled into Black neighbourhoods around 1900 was ___.
why: Tremé, of all places. They married locally, some of them took local names, and their selling routes ran across the South carrying embroidered cloth long before anybody thought of them as an immigrant community.

q: The first member of the US Congress with a Bangladeshi father represented the state of ___.
why: Hansen Clarke of Detroit, who served a single term. His father was a Bengali immigrant who died when Clarke was a child — which is why the first Bangladeshi-American in Congress does not carry a Bengali name.

q: New York's street carts selling chicken over rice are run mostly by Egyptians and ___.
why: The white sauce is American, the cart is Egyptian, and a great many of the men working them are Bangladeshi — recruited along the same village and family lines that fill the taxi ranks.

q: The Bengali-language weekly newspapers of the American diaspora are nearly all published in ___.
why: Several of them, competing hard, stacked by the door of every Bengali grocery from Queens to Buffalo — and read, mostly, for the community notices and the wedding photographs.

q: Manhattan's 'Curry Row', where the Indian restaurants were almost all Bangladeshi-run, is East ___ Street.
why: A single block of Indian restaurants where, for years, the owners and the kitchens were Sylheti and several of the businesses were run by relatives. Diners were handed an Indian menu by a family from Bangladesh, and nobody was exactly lying.

q: Before the lottery, most Bangladeshis who reached America arrived on a ___ visa.
why: Which is why the first generation in America skews so heavily to engineers, doctors and academics, and why the community's oldest associations were founded on university campuses rather than above shops.

q: The New York trade that absorbed a whole generation of Bangladeshi arrivals was driving a ___.
why: Nights, little English needed at the start, and a licence you could get in weeks — the same logic that put Sylhetis in British kitchens put Bangladeshis behind New York windscreens, and a whole social world grew up around the night shift.

q: The South Asian blocks of Jackson Heights are known above all for their windows full of ___.
why: Whole shopfronts of it, lit like an operating theatre and priced by weight — so the haggling is never about the design, only about the making charge on top.

q: The free online school watched by millions of students, founded by a Bangladeshi-American, is ___.
why: It started as maths videos recorded to help one cousin with her homework. The name on the door came from a father born in Bangladesh, which makes it quietly one of the most-used Bangladeshi surnames on earth.

q: A co-founder with a Bangladeshi father filmed and posted the very first video ever uploaded to ___.
why: Jawed Karim, born in Germany to a Bangladeshi father and a German mother, filmed nineteen seconds of himself at San Diego Zoo. It is still up, and it is still about elephants.

q: For a great many Bangladeshi families, the first American address in Queens was a rented ___.
why: Low ceilings, one window at pavement height, often two families and a rota for the kitchen. A decade later the same family is arguing about a driveway in Buffalo or a semi in Parkchester.

q: The men who go into the Sundarbans each spring to cut wild honeycomb are the ___.
why: They go in for a few weeks with a permit, a smoking torch and no protection worth the name, into the one forest in the world where the tiger genuinely hunts people. The bawali cut wood; the mouali take the honey.

q: Sundarbans woodcutters, Hindu and Muslim alike, ask permission of the forest deity ___.
why: One of the very few figures both communities pray to without renegotiating anything. The stories are performed as a folk drama, and Dakshin Rai — the tiger lord she keeps in check — is the antagonist.

q: The Sundarbans palm whose long leaves are cut for thatching roofs is ___.
why: A licensed harvest, cut and rafted out in bundles, and it roofs a very large number of houses in the south-west. The sap can also be tapped for gur, which makes it one of the few plants that roofs you and sweetens your tea.

q: Bangladesh's freshwater dolphin, nearly blind and navigating entirely by sound, is the ___.
why: The water it lives in is far too silty for eyes to be worth keeping, so it swims on its side, trailing a flipper along the bottom, listening. Passengers on a Barishal launch still see them roll past at dawn.

q: The only ape in Bangladesh, whooping through the canopy at Lawachara, is the ___.
why: An ape, not a monkey — no tail, and it swings rather than runs. Pairs call in duet at first light, which is how you find them, and the forest they need has been cut into pieces small enough to strand them.

q: Bangladesh's freshwater swamp forest, where you row a boat between the tree trunks, is ___.
why: For part of the year it is an ordinary wood you can walk through; in the monsoon the water comes up several metres and the same wood becomes navigable. The snakes sit in the branches, which is the detail everybody remembers.

q: The saucer-shaped wetland of the north-east that becomes an inland sea each monsoon is a ___.
why: In winter it is farmland with villages on raised mounds; in the monsoon those villages are islands and the school run is a boat. The submersible roads out there are built to be underwater for months and to survive it.

q: The Ramsar-listed haor of Sunamganj, famous for its winter birds, is ___.
why: It is managed under an international wetland treaty, which in practice means an argument between fishing rights and bird counts that has run for decades. The winter skyline over it is one of the sights of the country.

q: The great shrinking wetland spread across the Natore and Sirajganj districts is ___ Beel.
why: It was once so large that boats crossed it as a journey rather than an outing. Silt and embankments have taken most of it, and what is left is farmland for half the year and water for the other half.

q: The red-soil sal forest tract north of Dhaka, home to Garo villages, is ___.
why: A raised terrace of old red clay that the rivers never flattened, which is why it grows sal instead of rice. It is the closest thing to a forest within a couple of hours of Dhaka, and it is under permanent pressure from that fact.

q: In Bangladesh the sal tree, which gives Madhupur its forest, is also called the ___ tree.
why: Two names for one tree, which catches out anyone who learned the word in a schoolbook and then hears a forest guard use the other. It coppices from the stump, so a cut sal forest comes back — slowly, and thinner each time.

q: The temporary silt islands that surface and vanish in the big rivers are called ___.
why: People settle them within a season of their appearing, farm them, and lose them again — sometimes to the same river in the same decade. Whole communities have a word for themselves built on the land they know is temporary.

q: The Bengali word for a river eating its own bank and taking the houses with it is ___.
why: It is not flooding — flooding leaves and the land is still there. Bhangon takes the land itself, and families watch it come for weeks, dismantling and moving the house tin sheet by tin sheet.

q: The violent squalls that tear across the country in April, before the monsoon, are called ___.
why: Named for the month of Boishakh and for how black the sky goes. They arrive in the late afternoon, take the tin roofs and the mango crop with them, and are gone in half an hour.

q: Between autumn and winter the Bengali calendar keeps a whole season of its own, called ___.
why: Six seasons, not four — and hemanta is the one no translation handles, the short dry gap when the aman harvest comes in and before the cold arrives. It is also the season most Bengali poetry is homesick for.

q: The Bengali monsoon covers two months: Ashar and ___.
why: Ashar is the arrival and Shrabon is the one that does not stop — days of grey water and no shadow. Roughly half the songs anybody can name in Bengali are about one of these two months.

q: Bengali has two words for high water: bonna for the destructive kind, and ___ for the expected kind.
why: The distinction is the whole argument about the delta. Water arriving on time and going down again is what makes the soil; water arriving wrong is a disaster — and outside Bengali, both come out as the single word 'flood'.

q: The Ganges crosses into Bangladesh and changes its name to the ___.
why: A river with two names on two sides of a border, which makes water talks between the countries slower than they need to be. The Brahmaputra pulls the same trick and becomes the Jamuna.

q: At the border the Barak splits into two Sylhet rivers: the Kushiyara and the ___.
why: Sylhet town sits on the Surma, which is why 'Surma valley' turns up in old British records and in the name of half the restaurants in East London.

q: The river Dhaka grew up on, now black with tannery and dye waste, is the ___.
why: The name means 'old Ganges'. Sadarghat still puts out a hundred launches a day from its bank, and the water they push off from has been declared clinically dead more than once.

q: The one river in Bangladesh where carp still spawn naturally, and fishermen scoop up the eggs, is the ___.
why: Rui, katla and mrigal come up it to breed, and for a few nights each spring hundreds of boats wait to collect the fertilised eggs, which are then hatched in pits on the bank. It is the genetic stock the whole country's fish farming runs on.

q: Bangladesh's largest lake, made by damming the Karnaphuli, is ___.
why: It is entirely man-made, built for a hydroelectric station in the 1960s, and it drowned a great deal of the Chakma heartland including the royal palace. The tops of the old hills are the islands you see today.

q: The island in the Meghna estuary whose name means 'silent island', now full of spotted deer, is ___.
why: The deer were introduced deliberately — a handful released in the 1970s, now thousands. The mangrove around them was planted too, which makes the whole island a fairly recent piece of engineering pretending to be wilderness.

q: The only district of Bangladesh that is entirely an island is ___.
why: Sitting in the mouth of the Meghna, it loses land to the river at one end and gains it at the other. Its gas field supplies a good deal of the country and it still has no bridge to the mainland.

q: Bangladesh's only hilly island, just off Cox's Bazar, is ___.
why: Everything else offshore is flat silt; this one has a ridge, and on top of the ridge an old Shiva temple that pilgrims climb to. Betel leaf from the island is sold by name in Chittagong.

q: Saint Martin's Island is known locally as Narikel ___.
why: 'Coconut island' — and the palms are genuinely the first thing you see coming in. The name Saint Martin came from a British survey; almost nobody who lives there uses it.

q: The southern beach where you can watch both the sunrise and the sunset over water is ___.
why: It faces almost due south with open sea on both sides, which is the whole trick. The name means 'dug well', after the wells the Rakhine settlers sank there for fresh water.

q: Bangladesh's largest district by area, almost all of it hill and lake, is ___.
why: Largest by area and among the thinnest by population, which tells you most of what you need to know about it. Getting between two points inside the district often means a boat rather than a road.

q: From the far north of Bangladesh on a clear winter morning you can see the peak of ___.
why: From Tetulia in Panchagarh, across the Indian plain, for a few weeks a year when the haze lifts. People drive up from Dhaka for it and about half of them see nothing at all.

q: The dry, red-soil upland of the north-west, unusually short of water, is the ___ Tract.
why: A raised old terrace the rivers never got round to burying in silt, so it sits above the flood and misses the water everyone else complains about having too much of. It is the one part of the country where drought is the normal worry.

q: The northern river that gives Rangpur both its floods and its irrigation is the ___.
why: It rises in the Himalaya, arrives fast, and does most of its business in a few weeks. The barrage on it is the largest irrigation scheme in the country and the river it draws from is shared, which has kept it in the news for forty years.

q: The town at the meeting of the Padma and the Meghna, and capital of the ilish trade, is ___.
why: Two enormous rivers arriving at one point, and a fish market that sets the price everybody else argues with. Its claim to be the ilish capital has been disputed for a century without ever being beaten.

q: The Sylhet border valley where boats and men haul stones out of the riverbed is ___.
why: The stones wash down from the Meghalaya hills and are lifted out by hand, by the tonne, for concrete. It is one of the most photographed places in the country and one of the hardest ways to earn a living in it.

q: The irrigated dry-season rice crop that now feeds Bangladesh through the year is ___.
why: Aman is the old monsoon crop that depended on the rain arriving properly; boro is grown in the dry months on pumped groundwater and overtook it. The country's food security and its falling water table are the same story.

q: Jute earned Bengal its old nickname as the land of the ___ fibre.
why: The colour of the retted, dried fibre, and for a long stretch the country's main export earner. Sacking, rope, carpet backing and — after a Bangladeshi-led team sequenced its genome — a good deal of national pride.

q: The migratory birds that arrive on Bangladesh's lakes every winter are known in Bengali as ___ birds.
why: Not 'migratory' — guests. They come down from Siberia and the Himalaya to Tanguar Haor and the campus lakes at Jahangirnagar, and the word carries an obligation with it that 'migratory' does not.

q: The Sundarbans is not just a forest but a tidal one — twice a day the sea pushes ___ into it.
why: Everything in it is built for that: the breathing roots that stick up out of the mud, the seeds that germinate on the tree before dropping. The tiger swims between islands because at high water there is often no other way across.

q: The river that made Narayanganj a port and now carries its dye factories' outflow is the ___.
why: Narayanganj was called the Dundee of the East for its jute mills, and the river is why — deep enough for barges, close enough to Dhaka. The jute went; the factories and the outflow stayed.

q: The standing arrangement in a diaspora household: the parents speak Bengali and the children answer in ___.
why: Linguists have a name for it — receptive bilingualism. Everyone understands everyone, nobody has to switch, and the language quietly stops being spoken by the generation that still understands every word of it.

q: In a diaspora family, going to Bangladesh is never called a holiday — it is going to ___.
why: 'Desh' means country, and using it this way quietly settles which country is which. Children born abroad inherit the word and use it for a place they have visited four times.

q: Weekend Bangla school begins every child in the same place: the vowels, called the ___.
why: Eleven of them, chanted, before anyone gets near a consonant. The children who make it as far as juktakkhor — the compound letters — are the ones who can still read a signboard in Dhaka twenty years later.

q: The one ingredient no Bangladeshi kitchen contains, despite an entire industry abroad running on it, is ___.
why: It was invented for people who wanted one jar instead of nine. A Bangladeshi cook adds spices at four different points for four different reasons, which is precisely what a pre-mixed powder cannot do.

q: Every diaspora Bangladeshi house has a chest freezer, and the thing it exists for is ___.
why: Bought in bulk the day a shipment lands, cleaned in an assembly line in the kitchen, and stacked in labelled bags. The freezer in the garage is the single most reliable indicator of a Bangladeshi household anywhere on earth.

q: In Sylhet, a family with relatives settled in Britain is known as a ___ family.
why: It means Britain, not London, and it is a description of standing rather than geography. The tall, brightly painted, largely empty houses across Sylhet were built with that money, for a family that visits every few years.

q: Britain's Bangladeshi community has its own satellite television station, called Channel ___.
why: Broadcasting mostly in Sylheti to an audience that standard Bengali channels never really addressed — which is exactly why it worked. Its fundraising telethons for causes back home run for hours and raise a great deal.

q: A diaspora Bangladeshi association is usually called a ___, and its committee elections are legendary.
why: Every city with more than about forty Bangladeshi families has one, and several have two because of a disagreement nobody can now reconstruct. They organise the Eid hall, the mela and the funerals, and the elections are fought like a general election.

q: The video-calling app Bangladeshi families abroad use above all others is ___.
why: It worked on a bad connection and a cheap phone years before its rivals did, and once the grandmothers had it, nothing else stood a chance. Whole families abroad keep it installed for exactly one person.

q: The informal, off-the-books channel money is sent home through is called ___.
why: No money crosses a border: a man abroad takes cash, and a man in Bangladesh pays it out from his own float, and the two settle up later. It is faster, cheaper and completely untraceable, which is the whole of the argument about it.

q: Before internet calling, every diaspora kitchen drawer was full of cheap international ___ cards.
why: Sold from the corner shop, with a scratch panel, a long access number and a rate that got worse the longer you talked. A whole informal industry ran on them, and the whole thing evaporated inside about three years.

q: After the state school day, a great many diaspora Bangladeshi children went straight on to the ___.
why: An hour or two at the mosque, five days a week, learning to read a script in a language nobody in the room spoke. Bangla school was Sunday; this was the rest of the week.

q: Any older man in the community is 'bhai'; any slightly older woman is ___.
why: Aunty is a generation up and carries an accusation with it. Apu is the safe move for anyone within a decade of you, and getting the two the wrong way round is a genuine social injury.

q: Eid is not a public holiday in the West, so across the diaspora the day is taken as ___.
why: Booked months in advance against a date that moves with the moon and is not finally confirmed until the night before. New York's schools are one of the few places to have simply put it on the calendar.

q: A diaspora child's first lesson in reading ingredient labels is checking sweets for ___.
why: Marshmallows, wine gums, most jelly sweets and a surprising number of yoghurts. It is the reason a generation of children could read the back of a packet before they could read a menu.

q: Money earned abroad goes home and turns, first of all, into a ___.
why: Built in stages over years, wired for a family that mostly is not there, and standing several floors above its neighbours on purpose. After the house comes a mosque, and after the mosque an argument about land.

q: The one thing that keeps a diaspora family arguing with relatives back home for decades is ___.
why: Papers from three generations ago, a cousin who has been farming it since 1990, and a family abroad who paid for it and cannot get to a district court. Almost every probashi family has one and almost none of them are settled.

q: The appliance that never gets put away in a diaspora Bangladeshi kitchen is the ___.
why: On the counter, plugged in, with rice in it, permanently. The pressure cooker earns its place too but at least has the decency to live in a cupboard between uses.

q: Money sent home to Bangladesh spikes twice a year, in the weeks before the two ___.
alt: eid ul fitr and eid ul adha
why: New clothes for a household of eleven, the sacrifice animal, and something for everyone who asks. Bangladesh's monthly remittance figures have two visible bumps a year and both of them are moon-dated.

q: Marriage proposals circulate through the diaspora as a one-page document called a ___.
why: Height, education, complexion, family, and one photograph taken against a curtain. It is a CV for a person's whole life, forwarded through aunts, and the format has survived every dating app so far.

q: The airline the diaspora complains about constantly and books anyway is ___.
why: The word simply means aeroplane. It flies direct where the alternatives make you change in the Gulf, and that single fact has outweighed every complaint ever made about it.

q: In an immigrant Bangladeshi household the eldest child has an unpaid job title: family ___.
why: Doctor's appointments, letters from the council, the parents' evening where they translate their own report. It is the reason so many eldest children of that generation are unnervingly comfortable on the phone with officialdom.

q: Before streaming, the giveaway that a British street had Bangladeshi families was the ___ on the wall.
why: Bolted on at an angle that pointed at a specific satellite over the Indian Ocean, and put up by a man from the community who did the whole street. It carried the Bengali channels a decade before anyone could stream them.

q: Weekend Bangla school abroad is almost always run not by trained teachers but by ___.
why: Somebody's father with a whiteboard in a hired community hall, working from a textbook carried over in a suitcase. It is the entire infrastructure of language transmission in the diaspora, and it runs on goodwill and squash.

q: Diaspora Bangladeshis order naan in restaurants, but the bread actually made at home is ___.
why: Naan needs a tandoor, which is why it belongs to restaurants and not to houses. Ruti is flour, water and a hot tawa, made in a stack every evening, and the last one is always given to whoever is standing nearest.

q: Before a diaspora wedding, the family flies to Dhaka and comes back with a suitcase of ___.
why: The making charges are lower, the designs are the ones the mother-in-law actually wants, and the whole trip pays for itself. The saris come back too, but the gold is what the trip was for.

q: The diaspora community event that is really a market, a concert and a family reunion at once is the ___.
why: One field, a stage nobody can hear, forty stalls selling the same three things, and everybody you have ever met. The children complain the entire time and remember it for thirty years.

q: The Bengali monk who left Bikrampur to reform Buddhism in Tibet was ___.
why: He went in his late fifties, never came back, and is still one of the most revered figures in Tibetan Buddhism. Part of his remains were returned to Dhaka in 1978, which is a strange fate for a man from a village near Munshiganj.

q: The Narsingdi dig that pushed Bengal's urban history back by centuries is ___.
why: Two villages, a fort wall, silver punch-marked coins and beads that came a very long way. It turned a region assumed to be forest into a trading settlement contemporary with the earliest cities of the subcontinent.

q: The ridge of Buddhist monastery ruins outside Comilla is called ___.
why: More than fifty sites strung along one low ridge, of which Shalban Vihara is the one everyone visits. It was a working centre of Buddhist scholarship while Europe was still building in wood.

q: The Buddhist dynasty that ruled Bengal for some four centuries was the ___.
why: Under them Bengal exported scholars and sculpture across Asia, and the bronze style they developed turns up in Nepal, Tibet and Java. Very little of the empire survives above ground; almost all of it is dug up.

q: The first Pala king took the throne of Bengal not by birth or conquest but by ___.
why: Bengal had spent decades in a state the old texts call matsyanyaya — the rule of fish, big eating small — and the chiefs are said to have simply chosen Gopala to end it. It is one of the odder origin stories any dynasty has.

q: The dynasty that displaced the Buddhist Palas and ruled until the Turkish conquest was the ___.
why: They came from the south, brought orthodox Hinduism with them, and reorganised Bengali society along caste lines in a way that outlasted them by many centuries. Their last king lost his capital to a cavalry raid.

q: The Turkish commander who took Bengal at the start of the 13th century, with a famously tiny advance party, was ___.
why: The chronicles say he rode into the Sena capital ahead of his army and the guards took him for a horse dealer. Whether or not that is true, it is the version every schoolbook in Bengal prints.

q: The sultan who first pulled Bengal's rival kingdoms into one and styled himself Shah-i-Bangalah was ___.
why: The title matters more than the man: it is the first time the whole delta is described as one country with one name, and 'Bangalah' is where the word Bengal comes from.

q: The Sultanate-era 'Small Golden Mosque' stands among the ruins of Gaur, in ___ district.
why: Gaur was one of the great cities of medieval India and the border now runs straight through it, leaving half its monuments on either side. The gilding that gave the mosque its name is long gone.

q: The finest grade of Dhaka muslin was called abrawan, which means ___.
why: The names of the grades were the sales pitch: abrawan for running water, shabnam for evening dew. Laid on wet grass, the cloth was said to be invisible — which is a claim, but the surviving pieces do not embarrass it.

q: Dhaka muslin could only be spun from one variety of cotton, called ___.
why: A short, difficult cotton that grew along the Meghna and nowhere else worth mentioning, spun in the damp of early morning because the thread snapped in dry air. When the trade collapsed the plant went with it, and reviving it has taken decades of work.

q: The dye crop Bengali peasants were forced to grow, and in 1859 refused to plant, was ___.
why: It paid the planter well and the grower almost nothing, on land that could have grown rice. The refusal spread village by village across Bengal and is remembered as one of the first mass acts of organised refusal in the country.

q: The 1860 Bengali play about the indigo planters, whose English translation got its publisher jailed, was ___.
why: The missionary who published the translation, James Long, was fined and imprisoned for a month — and a Bengali writer paid the fine on the spot in open court. The play is mediocre theatre and enormous history.

q: The 1757 battle that handed Bengal to the East India Company was fought at ___.
why: It lasted a few hours and was decided before it started, by an arrangement with the Nawab's own commander. The Bengali name, Palashi, comes from the palash tree — the flame of the forest.

q: The last independent Nawab of Bengal, defeated at Plassey, was ___.
why: He was about twenty-three, had been on the throne barely a year, and inherited a court that had already decided against him. His name survives in Bengali mostly as shorthand for being sold out from the inside.

q: When the Mughals made Dhaka their provincial capital, they renamed it ___.
why: Named for the emperor of the day, in 1610, by a governor who moved the capital here to be closer to the rivers he needed to police. The name lasted about a century; the university outside Dhaka still carries it.

q: The Mughal fort in Old Dhaka, abandoned unfinished after a governor's daughter died there, is ___.
why: Pari Bibi's tomb sits in the middle of it, and the fort was declared unlucky and left as it stood. Three centuries later it is the only large green space in that part of Dhaka, which is a use nobody intended.

q: Old Dhaka's Star Mosque is covered in thousands of pieces of broken ___.
why: The technique is called chinitikri, and the mosque got its coat of it in the 1930s from a local businessman who imported crockery specifically to smash. Look closely and you will find whole Japanese Mount Fuji plates set into the wall.

q: The Old Dhaka quarter of Armanitola is named after its community of ___ traders.
why: They dealt in jute and salt, built a church there in 1781 that still stands, and were rich enough that a Dhaka Armenian once part-owned the city's water supply. The last of the congregation left decades ago; the graves did not.

q: Everyday Bengali words like janala, almari, chabi and balti were all borrowed from ___.
why: The Portuguese were in Bengal a century before the British and left almost nothing behind except vocabulary — window, cupboard, key, bucket, and the word for a table. Also, quietly, the technique for making chhana, which is most of Bengali sweet-making.

q: The Mughal governor who took Chittagong from the Arakanese in 1666 was ___.
why: He is remembered in Dhaka less for the campaign than for the price of rice: the story goes that he walled up a city gate and swore it would not open until eight maunds again cost a rupee. It has not opened.

q: The abandoned street of merchant mansions at Sonargaon is called ___.
why: About fifty houses on one narrow lane, built by cloth traders in the 19th century and emptied within a couple of generations. It is the most photographed ruin in the country and one bad monsoon away from being much less of one.

q: The confederacy of chieftains who held the delta against the Mughals were known as the ___.
why: 'Twelve landholders', though the number is more of a figure of speech than a census. Isa Khan of Sonargaon is the one everyone names, and the marshes and rivers did most of the actual fighting on their behalf.

q: The 18th-century Dinajpur temple covered in thousands of terracotta plaques is the ___ Temple.
why: Every surface is baked clay panels, and the subjects run from the epics to a European in a hat with a rifle. It lost its nine spires to an earthquake in the 19th century and has never had them back.

q: The Sultanate mosque of Rajshahi district famous for its terracotta panels stands at ___.
why: Brick, not stone, because Bengal has no stone worth quarrying — so the decoration had to be pressed and fired instead of carved. That single geological fact is why Bengali architecture looks like nothing else in South Asia.

q: In 1905 the British split Bengal in two and made ___ the capital of the new eastern province.
why: The split lasted six years before being reversed, but those six years gave Dhaka a secretariat, a High Court and the beginnings of a claim to be a capital city rather than a district town. Curzon Hall was built in the middle of it.

q: Dhaka University opened in 1921 and was known for decades as the Oxford of the ___.
why: Founded partly as compensation for undoing the 1905 partition, on a campus of Mughal ruins and colonial bungalows. For a long stretch it was the only route out of rural East Bengal that did not involve a ship.

q: The Moroccan traveller who came to Sylhet in the 1340s to meet Shah Jalal was ___.
why: He walked in from Chittagong, spent three days, and left a description of Bengal as a place of astonishing cheapness and unpleasant damp — 'a hell full of good things', as the phrase is usually rendered.

q: The grey pigeons that live around Shah Jalal's shrine in Sylhet are called ___.
why: Descended, the story goes, from a pair given to the saint, and nobody in Sylhet will harm one. They are on the crest of the local football team and unofficially on the city itself.

q: The Chittagong shrine famous for the pond of rare turtles in its courtyard is ___.
why: The turtles are a black soft-shell species that survives essentially nowhere else, kept alive for centuries by visitors feeding them bananas. Biologists spent years arguing about them before conceding the shrine had done a better job than any reserve.

q: The word 'taka' comes down from a medieval silver coin called the ___.
why: Struck by the Delhi and Bengal sultans, and the name stuck so hard in Bengali that rupees were called taka for two centuries before the currency officially was. Bengalis still say taka for any money, anywhere.

q: The Bengali calendar was reworked under the Mughals so that tax could be collected after the ___.
why: The lunar Hijri year drifts against the seasons, so tax demands kept arriving when farmers had nothing. Pinning the year to the solar seasons fixed that — which is why Pohela Boishakh is, underneath the festival, an accounting date.

q: Old Dhaka's Shankhari Bazar is named for craftsmen who cut bangles out of ___.
why: The shells come from the far south of India, are sawn by hand into white bangles, and are worn by married Hindu women. The lane is about three metres wide, four centuries old, and still doing the same job.

q: One long-standing story has it that Dhaka takes its name from the ___ temple.
why: The rival explanations are just as good: the dhak tree, or the dhak drum a sultan supposedly had beaten to mark the city's limits. Nobody can settle it, which has not stopped anybody asserting it.

q: The great Mughal caravanserai on the Buriganga bank, now half-swallowed by Old Dhaka, is the ___ Katra.
why: Built as lodging for travellers with the rents endowed to maintain it in perpetuity — an arrangement that lasted rather less than perpetuity. Shops are now built into its arches and much of it has simply been absorbed.

q: The 18th-century woman who ran one of Bengal's largest estates from Natore was Rani ___.
why: Widowed young and left holding an estate that covered a good part of northern Bengal, she is remembered for the temples, roads and rest houses she built with it. Locally she is still called Ardha-Bangeshwari — ruler of half of Bengal.

q: The Mughal-era Shia hall in Old Dhaka, from which the Muharram procession sets out, is ___.
why: Dhaka's Shia community has been small for centuries and its imambara is one of the oldest buildings still in continuous use in the city. The procession that leaves it each year draws a crowd far larger than the community.

q: Before the British, Dhaka muslin's most reliable buyers were the courts of ___.
why: The imperial household took the best of it by right, before any of it reached a market — a standing order that kept the finest weavers employed and the finest grades effectively unbuyable. When the court fell, that top tier of the craft had nowhere to go.

q: The Brick Lane mosque was built as a Huguenot chapel and then spent seventy years as a ___.
why: One building, three communities, in the order they arrived on that street: French Protestant weavers, then Jewish refugees, then Sylhetis. Nobody designed it as a monument to migration and it is the best one in London.

q: The sundial on the Brick Lane mosque is carved 'Umbra Sumus', which means we are ___.
why: Put there by the Huguenots in 1743, and it has outlasted every congregation that has read it. Anybody who has stood under it during a Brick Lane afternoon will tell you it is doing rather a lot of work for two words.

q: In 2009 the Brick Lane mosque gained a modern stainless-steel ___ beside it.
why: Twenty-nine metres of illuminated steel bolted onto a Georgian chapel, and the first thing on that building in three hundred years that announces from the outside what it is now used for.

q: Before the restaurants, the East End trade that employed most Bangladeshi men was the ___ trade.
why: Machining in small workshops around Fashion Street and Hanbury Street, on the same floors where Jewish tailors had worked a generation earlier. When the work went abroad in the 1980s the same men went into kitchens.

q: Sylhetis came to dominate British ships because hiring was controlled by a crew boss called the ___.
why: He recruited from his own village and his own relatives, so one district's men filled the engine rooms and everyone else's did not. Almost the entire British Bangladeshi community exists because of that hiring practice.

q: The first Bengali institutions in the East End were not shops or mosques but seamen's ___.
why: Run by men who had come off the ships themselves, around Aldgate and Cable Street, and doubling as post office, employment agency and bank. Everything the community built afterwards started from an address like that.

q: The pioneer who ran a Commercial Road café and helped a generation of Sylheti seamen settle was Ayub Ali ___.
why: 'Master' because he taught men to read and fill in forms. His café doubled as a hostel and an address for letters, and a great many people's first week in Britain began at his table.

q: In the late 1970s Bengali families in the East End won housing by organising to ___ empty council flats.
why: Families were being placed on estates where they did not feel safe, and refusing them meant being marked as intentionally homeless. Organising to occupy blocks together, rather than take flats singly, was the answer they arrived at, and it worked.

q: At the north end of Brick Lane, the last survivors of the Jewish East End are two ___ shops.
why: Open around the clock, next door to each other, and locked in a rivalry that has outlasted the community that started them. The queue at four in the morning is half nightclub and half taxi drivers.

q: The great brick complex halfway up Brick Lane, once a brewery, is now the ___.
why: It brewed on that site for two and a half centuries and was once the largest brewery in the world. It is now market stalls and studios, and it is the exact point on the street where the curry houses stop and the coffee starts.

q: Tower Hamlets holds Britain's largest Bangladeshi population and, a mile away, the towers of ___.
why: Built on the docks the first Sylheti seamen sailed into. Two of the highest concentrations of money and of child poverty in the country, inside one local authority, sharing a set of bus routes.

q: Tower Hamlets rebranded its public libraries with the unusual name ___.
why: The reasoning was that people who would not walk into a library would walk into a shop, so they were put on the high street next to the supermarkets and opened on Sundays. Borrowing went up sharply, and the name is still mocked.

q: Tower Hamlets is named for the hamlets that once owed service to the ___.
why: The hamlets outside the city wall were obliged to supply men for the Tower's guard, and the collective name for them stuck for six hundred years until it was handed to a modern borough.

q: The East London Mosque began life in 1910 as an endowment called the London Mosque ___.
why: Decades of rented rooms and temporary halls before there was a building, let alone the one on Whitechapel Road now. It predates the Bangladeshi community that fills it by about half a century.

q: The 1936 confrontation that East Enders still commemorate with a mural happened on ___ Street.
why: Jewish, Irish and dockworking East Enders blocked a fascist march through their streets, and the mural went up forty years later. It is quoted constantly by the Bangladeshi East End, which arrived afterwards and inherited the argument.

q: Around Brick Lane the street signs carry the name twice: once in English and once in ___.
why: A council decision from the 1990s, made at the same time as the Banglatown branding, and one of very few places in Britain where a community's script is on the official signage. Visitors photograph them; residents stopped noticing years ago.

q: The most repeated origin story for chicken tikka masala places its invention in ___.
why: A customer sent his chicken tikka back as too dry, and the chef is said to have opened a tin of tomato soup. Every part of that is disputed and none of it has ever been disproved, which is why the story has outlived the argument.

q: British curry houses have been closing in numbers largely because they cannot recruit ___.
why: Visa rules closed the route from Sylhet, and the British-born generation went into other work. A trade that ran for fifty years on chain migration from a handful of villages has no obvious second act.

q: Curry house owners will tell you the trade is finishing because their children went to ___.
why: The restaurant paid for the degree and the degree emptied the restaurant. It is the most complete generational success story in the diaspora and it reads, from behind the counter, like a loss.

q: The city that has taken the Curry Capital of Britain title more often than any other is ___.
why: Won repeatedly, and defended with the seriousness of a football result. The joke inside the trade is that Bradford's curry is mostly Pakistani-run, so the Bangladeshi restaurateurs who dominate the rest of the country keep losing a prize named after their own industry.

q: Bradford's huge South Asian community is overwhelmingly not Bangladeshi but ___.
why: Mostly from Mirpur in Kashmir, on the same mills-and-chain-migration pattern that brought Sylhetis to Oldham. Outsiders read every northern British Asian community as the same one; nobody inside them does.

q: Leicester's Belgrave Road, its sweet shops and its Diwali lights belong to a community that is largely ___.
why: Many of them came from East Africa in the 1970s rather than directly from India, which is why the community arrived with shops and capital rather than shift work. It is the clearest counter-example to the idea of a single British Asian story.

q: Bangladeshis came to Oldham and Rochdale for night-shift work in the ___.
why: The mills could only stay profitable running around the clock, and the night shift was the one nobody local wanted. Within twenty years the mills had gone and the community they recruited had not.

q: Luton's South Asian community grew up around shift work at the town's ___ plant.
why: A single employer big enough to shape a town's population. The same pattern repeats across the Midlands and the North — a factory recruits, a village follows, and the factory closes long before the community does.

q: Cardiff's old dockside quarter, home to Bengali, Somali and Yemeni seamen, was known as ___.
why: One of the oldest multiracial communities in Britain, built on coal exports and the crews who carried them. Bengali seamen were part of it long before there was a Bangladeshi Britain to speak of, and most of the old streets were demolished in the 1960s.

q: Birmingham's balti houses were founded mostly by Kashmiri and ___ families, not Bangladeshi ones.
why: The one significant British curry style the Bangladeshi trade did not invent, which is precisely why Birmingham insists on it. Served in the pressed steel bowl it was cooked in, with a naan the size of the table.

q: Manchester's Curry Mile is now dominated less by curry houses than by ___ cafés.
why: Middle Eastern and North African businesses moved in as the South Asian restaurants thinned out, and the street is busier at midnight than it ever was at dinner. The name has stayed regardless.

q: The lager created specifically to be drunk with a curry in Britain is ___.
why: Designed to be less gassy so a pint would not fill you up before the food arrived, and sold restaurant by restaurant out of the back of a car in the early years. A business built entirely on the Bangladeshi curry trade's distribution network.

q: Every British curry house meal begins, whether or not anybody ordered it, with ___.
why: With the tray of lime pickle, mango chutney, onion salad and that unplaceable red sauce. It appears on the bill afterwards, which every regular knows and nobody ever contests.

q: In Cockney rhyming slang, a curry is a 'Ruby ___'.
why: After a Northern Irish singer who was enormously famous in the 1950s and is now remembered almost entirely for this. A dish brought by Sylheti sailors, named after a Belfast pop star, in the slang of the East End.
