q: The curry house's hottest dish, invented in Britain and unknown in Bangladesh, is the ___.
why: Built for customers who wanted something above vindaloo and would order it as a dare. No cook in Bangladesh has heard of it, and no cook in Britain has ever been asked to eat one.

q: Vindaloo, on every British curry house menu, began as a ___ dish.
why: From carne de vinha d'alhos — meat in wine and garlic — which the Portuguese brought to Goa and Goa improved with chilli. The British curry house kept the name and replaced the wine with vinegar and the point with heat.

q: The curry house 'bhuna' takes its name from the Bengali word for ___.
why: Bhuna is a method — spices and onion fried down hard until the oil separates out — not a recipe. The British menu turned a verb into a dish, which is a fair summary of what happened to the whole cuisine.

q: The dish called do-piaza is named for having a double quantity of ___.
why: 'Do' is two and 'piaza' is onion — added at two different stages, fried at the start and again near the end. It is one of the few curry-house names that still describes what is actually in the pan.

q: The jalfrezi's name begins with the Bengali word jhal, which means ___.
why: It began as an Anglo-Indian way of frying up yesterday's cold roast with chilli and onion — a leftovers dish that climbed the menu. The 'frezi' part is generally traced to a word for stew.

q: The English word 'curry' is usually traced back to the Tamil word ___.
why: Picked up by the Portuguese in the south, carried into English, and then applied to the food of an entire subcontinent that had never used one word for it. No Bangladeshi cook has ever made a thing called curry.

q: British curry houses kept serving late into the night specifically to catch customers leaving the ___.
why: Eleven o'clock closing created a hungry crowd and nowhere else to feed it, and restaurants run by men who did not drink built an industry on the drinking hours of a country that did.

q: The wholesale warehouse every British curry house buys its supplies from is called a ___.
why: Twenty-kilo sacks, catering tins and no delivery — you turn up in a van at six in the morning. Several of the biggest are themselves Bangladeshi-owned, which is where a good deal of the trade's actual wealth ended up.

q: Britain's oldest surviving Indian restaurant, opened on Regent Street in 1926, is ___.
why: Founded to feed retired colonial officers who missed the food, decades before the Sylheti restaurants that would define the trade. It is still open and still expensive, which was always the point of it.

q: The black-tie annual event that made the British curry trade politically visible is the British Curry ___.
why: Prime ministers attend it, which tells you how much of the industry is Bangladeshi-owned and how much of it votes. Regional trophies, a live band, and a room full of people who will be back in a kitchen the next evening.

q: The thing that has changed the British curry trade most in the past decade is the ___ app.
why: It took the commission, the customer relationship and the reason for having a dining room, all at once. Restaurants that survived by being the only Indian in town discovered they were now competing with every other one in the county.

q: The night before Eid, when the moon is sighted and nobody goes to bed, is ___.
why: Mehendi on every girl's hands, the last impossible round of shopping, and the bangle stalls open past midnight. It is arguably better than Eid itself and everybody knows it.

q: The sweet vermicelli in milk served in every house on Eid morning is ___.
why: You will eat it in eight houses before noon and be judged on how much you leave in the bowl. The dry roasted kind and the milky kind divide households, and both will be offered before you get through the door.

q: Bangladeshis name the two Eids for what happens at them: Rojar Eid and ___ Eid.
why: Fasting Eid and sacrifice Eid — the names describe the work rather than the theology. Nobody in a Bangladeshi household says Eid al-Fitr out loud unless they are reading it off a form.

q: Korbani meat is divided three ways: for the household, for relatives, and for ___.
why: A third each, weighed out and sent round the neighbourhood in bags before anybody's own pot goes on. The hides are a separate matter again — they are usually given to a madrasa, which sells them.

q: Before Eid prayers, every household must pay a small compulsory charity called ___.
why: Reckoned per head, including the children, and set each year against the price of a staple food so it stays worth the same thing. Zakat is annual and on wealth; fitra is small, universal and has a deadline of about nine in the morning.

q: After Eid prayers, Bangladeshi men greet each other with a three-part embrace called ___.
why: Right shoulder, left shoulder, right again, with everyone in the field, including several men you have been avoiding all year. It is the single most efficient conflict-resolution mechanism in the culture.

q: Whether Eid falls tomorrow or the day after is announced by the national ___ committee.
why: They meet after sunset, take reports from across the country, and announce on television to a nation with its dinner going cold. Bangladesh usually lands a day behind Saudi Arabia, which has kept at least one argument alive in every family abroad.

q: The Bangladeshi iftar plate is built on chhola, muri, beguni and ___.
why: Split lentils, onion and chilli, fried in batches all afternoon. The whole plate is then mixed together with the muri by hand into something with no name, which is how it is actually eaten.

q: On the night of Shab-e-Barat, Bangladeshi households make and send round ruti and ___.
why: Semolina, carrot, egg or gram flour — usually several kinds, on a tray under a cloth, carried between houses by children all evening. The night is spent in prayer and the neighbourhood exchanges roughly the same food in circles.

q: The five-day autumn festival that fills Bangladeshi Hindu neighbourhoods with pandals and drums is ___.
why: The biggest festival of the Bangladeshi Hindu year by a distance, with thousands of temporary pandals across the country and a public holiday around it. The dhak drum is played by hereditary drummers who travel for the season.

q: Durga Puja ends when the clay images are carried to the river and given to the water — the ___.
why: The images are unfired clay from the riverbank, made to dissolve back into it — the whole festival is designed to end with nothing left. Married women send her off with sindoor first, which is the part everyone photographs.

q: The spring festival at which Bangladeshi Hindu students lay their books before the goddess is ___.
why: Books and instruments go at her feet the night before and may not be touched until the puja is done — a religious obligation not to study, which no student has ever needed explaining twice.

q: At the festival of Bhai Phota, a sister marks her brother's forehead and he owes her ___.
why: The mark is made with sandal paste and dew, and the vow spoken over it asks that death stay away from his door. He turns up with a present, which is the part the household actually negotiates about.

q: Bangladesh's Buddhist communities keep a national holiday for Buddha ___.
why: Purnima means full moon, and the day marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death all at once. It is a public holiday in a country whose Buddhist population is small and very old — Bengal was Buddhist for four centuries under the Palas.

q: Bangladeshi Christians call Christmas ___, which translates simply as 'the big day'.
why: A public holiday in Bangladesh, kept most visibly by Garo and Santal Christian villages and by the old Portuguese-descended families of Dhaka. Star lanterns go up over the lanes of Tejgaon and the cake is fruitcake.

q: For the fortnight before Eid-ul-Azha, Dhaka's open ground fills with temporary ___ markets.
why: Bamboo pens on every spare lot, farmers sleeping beside their animals for a week, and prices that swing wildly on the final night. The largest bulls are given names and get on television.

q: Old Dhaka's Chawkbazar Ramadan market is famous above all for its outsized ___.
why: Coils the size of a dinner plate, fried in vats on the pavement from mid-afternoon. The whole market runs for a few hours a day for one month a year and has done so for generations.

q: In Old Dhaka, groups still walk the lanes before dawn in Ramadan singing to wake people for ___.
why: The songs are called kasida, sung in groups with a drum, and the practice is older than alarm clocks and has outlived them. Residents complain about it every year and would riot if it stopped.

q: Bangladesh's largest Eid congregation gathers in an open field at ___.
why: A field in Kishoreganj that takes a crowd measured in the hundreds of thousands, with special trains laid on to reach it. The prayer is signalled by gunshot, because no sound system carries to the back.

q: Bangladeshi television marks each Eid with a solid week of specially made ___.
why: Dozens of one-off dramas, shot in a hurry, released across every channel and now every streaming platform. It is the single biggest week of the year for Bangladeshi actors and the reason nobody leaves the sofa on Eid afternoon.

q: In the days before Eid, Dhaka empties as millions leave the city for their ___.
why: Bus tickets sell out weeks ahead, launches leave Sadarghat overloaded, and men ride on the roofs of trains. For a few days the loudest city in the country is quiet enough to hear birds in.

q: The town near Dhaka whose enormous wooden chariot is hauled through the streets each Rath Jatra is ___.
why: Pulled by hand on ropes by whoever grabs one, in a crowd that has never been only Hindu. The original chariot was lost and the replacement was built with Indian help, which took years and a good deal of diplomacy.

q: At the Buddhist festival of Probarona, the night sky over Chittagong fills with ___.
why: Hot-air lanterns launched in their thousands from monastery courtyards, drifting for miles. They have since been borrowed by wedding parties across the country, to the considerable irritation of the fire service.

q: At Kathin Chibar Dan, Buddhist villagers spin, weave and dye a monk's robe within ___.
why: Cotton to finished robe, start to finish, by relays of women working through the night while the monastery waits. The point is precisely the difficulty — the offering is the labour, not the cloth.

q: The Marma new year in the Hill Tracts is celebrated by throwing ___ over each other.
why: Young men and women throw water at each other from a boat-shaped trough, and the water is understood to wash off the old year. It is the same festival family as Thailand's Songkran, marking the same solar new year the Bengali calendar does.

q: Old Dhaka marks the last day of the month of Poush by filling the sky with ___.
why: Every roof in the old city, all afternoon, with the string glassed to cut down other people's kites. It has acquired sound systems and fire-breathers in recent years, which the purists on the neighbouring roof will tell you about at length.

q: The harvest festival at which the first of the new rice is cooked and shared is ___.
why: The word means 'new rice'. It falls in the short dry season of Hemanta, when the aman crop comes in, and it is the one festival in the calendar with no religion attached to it at all — only the harvest.

q: On Pohela Boishakh, shopkeepers settle the old year's debts and open a new account book called the ___.
why: Customers are invited in, given sweets, and expected to clear what they owe — a debt collection dressed as hospitality, and far more effective than a letter. The ledger is red, bound in cloth, and started fresh that morning.

q: On Pohela Falgun, the first day of spring, Dhaka dresses almost entirely in ___.
why: Yellow saris, marigolds in the hair, and every park in the city photographed to death by lunchtime. It is a modern invention — barely a few decades old — and is now observed more thoroughly than festivals ten times its age.

q: Every February, Dhaka gives over a month to the country's enormous ___ fair.
why: Publishers hold back their entire year's list for it, so a Bangladeshi novel is far likelier to appear in February than in any other month. It grew out of one man selling books on a footpath and now covers acres.

q: On the morning of 21 February, people walk to the monument with flowers and, by tradition, ___.
why: The walk is called prabhat feri and the song sung on it is known by everybody in the country. Shoes come off at the edge of the ground, which is why the approach roads are lined with piles of them.

q: In Bangladeshi English, New Year's Eve is universally called ___ Night.
why: Nobody says New Year's Eve. It refers only to the English calendar's new year, never Pohela Boishakh, and it is one of those phrases that instantly identifies where somebody learned their English.

q: Every Bengali gets two names: the formal bhalo naam, and the one the household actually uses, the ___ naam.
why: Bubun, Tumpa, Rana, Mishti — a name nobody outside the family is supposed to hear, attached to a grown adult for life. Diaspora children usually get a third one as well, for teachers who cannot manage either.

q: Your father's brother is chacha; your mother's brother is ___.
why: English collapses eight relationships into 'uncle' and Bengali refuses to. Which side, which order of birth, blood or marriage — the word tells you before anybody explains, which is exactly why the diaspora's 'uncle' feels so thin.

q: Your mother's sister is khala; your father's sister is ___.
why: And their husbands get their own words again — khalu and fufa. Bengali Hindu households run a parallel set entirely: mashi and pishi. Nobody has ever needed a diagram and everybody has occasionally wanted one.

q: Your father's parents are dada and dadi; your mother's parents are ___.
why: Two sets, never confused, and the maternal house — nanar bari — is where a Bangladeshi childhood's summers happen. It is the one house where a child outranks the rules.

q: In a Bengali family the eldest is boro and the second is mejo, which makes the third ___.
why: Boro, mejo, shejo, no, and choto at the end however many arrived in between. The names attach to the aunts and uncles for life, so a woman of seventy is still Mejo Khala to a room of people who have never used her actual name.

q: The word for your child's spouse's father — a relationship English cannot name at all — is ___.
why: Two men who have nothing in common except a wedding, permanently and formally related, with a word for it and a slightly wary tone reserved for using it. Their wives are beyan to each other and generally get on far better.

q: The crowd of relatives who travel with the groom to the wedding are the ___.
why: Counted, catered for, and negotiated over in advance — a headcount too high is remembered by the bride's family for a generation. They arrive late by convention and are fed first by obligation.

q: The sum written into a Bangladeshi Muslim marriage contract as the bride's own right is the ___.
why: It is hers, not the family's, and it is a condition of the marriage rather than a gift. Half the negotiation before a wedding is about the figure, and a good deal of the argument afterwards is about whether it was ever actually paid.

q: The person who brings two families together for a marriage, and takes credit forever, is the ___.
why: Usually an aunt, occasionally a professional, and never entirely disinterested. The kazi registers the marriage; the ghotok caused it, and will remind both families of that at every event for thirty years.

q: The heavy woven sari a Bangladeshi bride traditionally wears is a ___.
why: Named for Benares, though Mirpur in Dhaka has been weaving them for decades — the neighbourhood is literally called Benarasi Palli. Red, gold, and heavy enough that the bride's posture in every photograph is doing real work.

q: The farewell meal cooked for someone on their last day of being unmarried is ___.
why: Every favourite dish at once, cooked by relatives in the days before the wedding, with the person being married sat down and fed like a child. The name means the rice of the unmarried, and it is the last meal in that house on those terms.

q: At a Bangladeshi wedding, the bride's younger cousins will steal the groom's ___ and charge to return them.
why: A negotiation conducted by twelve-year-olds with a wildly inflated opening price and no intention of compromising. The groom's side budgets for it, and losing the haggle graciously is part of the performance.

q: A Bangladeshi Muslim wedding turns on the bride and groom each saying one word: ___.
why: Said three times, in front of witnesses, and that is the marriage — everything else is catering. The room goes completely silent for it and then, without fail, somebody's phone rings.

q: At a Bengali Hindu wedding the couple first look at each other's faces reflected in a ___.
why: The betel leaves come down and they see each other in the mirror before they see each other directly. It is called shubho drishti, the auspicious glance, and it is the one moment of the day nobody has to be told to be quiet for.

q: A young Bangladeshi greets an elder at Eid or a wedding by touching their ___.
why: Called salam kora in Muslim households and pranam in Hindu ones, and answered by a hand on the head. The elder always half-stops you, and you always do it anyway; the negotiation is the whole point.

q: Handing something to a Bangladeshi elder, the one thing you must never use is your ___ hand.
why: The left is the bathroom hand and that is the end of the discussion. Left-handed children were once retrained out of it entirely, and a left-handed adult still hands over money with a small apologetic movement.

q: You do not enter a Bangladeshi house empty-handed; the safe default is a box of ___.
why: Two kilos, in a white cardboard box tied with string, and it will be opened, offered back to you, and half of it sent home with somebody else. Fruit is acceptable; arriving with nothing is discussed after you leave.

q: If your foot accidentally touches a book, a Bangladeshi child is taught to immediately touch it to their ___.
why: Books, money and rice all get the same apology. It is taught before the reason is, so grown adults do it automatically in an airport and cannot always say why.

q: A black smudge of kajal is put on a Bangladeshi baby's cheek to keep off the ___.
why: Deliberately placed off-centre, to spoil the perfection that would attract the wrong kind of attention. Praise a baby too warmly in a Bangladeshi house and somebody will quietly add a second smudge.

q: Bangladeshi households hold that you must never sweep the floor after ___.
why: Sweeping after dark sweeps the household's fortune out with the dust. The rule survives in flats with vacuum cleaners and grandmothers who will say nothing but will look at you.

q: If somebody sneezes just as you are leaving the house, you are supposed to ___.
why: Sit, count to a slow ten, drink something if there is anything to drink, then go. Nobody believes it and everybody does it, which is the working definition of a household superstition.

q: The old saying holds that a Bengali is made of two things: fish and ___.
why: Mache bhate Bangali. It is quoted as a description and used as an instruction, and it is why a plate with no fish on it registers to a Bengali eye as an unfinished meal rather than a different one.

q: The Bengali word for long, aimless, argumentative conversation pursued as a pastime is ___.
why: Not a chat and not a debate — it has no subject, no purpose and no natural end, and treating it as a waste of time marks you out immediately. Whole literary movements came out of it and so has every tea stall in the country.

q: The heavy afternoon sleep that follows a full plate of rice is called ___ ghum.
why: 'Rice sleep' — a named, expected, defended institution, not an accident. Ring a Bangladeshi house at three in the afternoon and somebody will answer in a whisper.

q: In Bengali, asking whether somebody has eaten at all is literally asking whether they have eaten ___.
why: Bhaat kheyecho? Answer 'I had a sandwich' and you have not answered the question. It is the standard greeting in half the country, and it means are you all right rather than are you hungry.

q: The thin checked cotton cloth used as towel, headwrap, filter, bag and belt is a ___.
why: Red and white, usually, and it dries in about ten minutes in a country where a proper towel never dries at all. It has become a design motif on aeroplanes and hotel lobbies, which amuses everyone who grew up with one.

q: The garment a Bangladeshi man changes into the moment he gets home is the ___.
why: A tube of checked cotton, retied about forty times a day, and structurally incompatible with sitting on a chair in a dignified manner. Diaspora households keep them, wear them strictly indoors, and never answer the door in one.

q: The thing hung over a Bangladeshi bed every single night, tucked in on all four sides, is the ___.
why: Hooked to four points in the ceiling and tucked under the mattress with a thoroughness usually reserved for surgery. One mosquito trapped inside it at midnight is a household emergency with a full search operation.

q: The plastic water jug that stands in the corner of every Bangladeshi bathroom is a ___.
why: Usually red, always plastic now, and the first thing a family carries into a new house abroad. Households that have installed a bidet keep it anyway, on the reasonable grounds that plumbing fails.

q: The wooden rack in a Bangladeshi bedroom, permanently buried under worn-once clothes, is the ___.
why: Not clean enough for the almari and not dirty enough for the wash — an entire category of clothing that exists only on the alna. Every household has one and every household denies its condition.

q: Rice and curry are properly eaten with the fingers of the ___ hand.
why: Mixing is half the meal — the dal into the rice, the fish broken in, everything judged by feel before it is tasted. Bengalis abroad will use a fork all week and eat with their hand the moment there is fish on the plate.

q: The first serious skill a Bangladeshi child is expected to master at the table is dealing with fish ___.
why: Bengali fish are full of fine bones and nobody fillets anything, so the sorting is done in the mouth, one-handed, while talking. Children abroad who were raised on salmon are found out the first time a rui appears.

q: In a traditional Bangladeshi household, the person who sits down to eat last is the ___.
why: After everyone has been served, seconds offered twice, and the fish counted. Ask about it and you will be told there was plenty — which is true often enough that nobody in the family can prove otherwise.

q: Bangladeshi tea is not brewed and then milked: the leaves, milk and sugar are all ___ together.
why: In one pan, until it climbs the sides, then poured through a strainer from a height. Handing a Bangladeshi guest a mug of hot water and a teabag on a saucer is a small, silent act of hostility.

q: After the Chakma, the largest Indigenous people of the Chittagong Hill Tracts are the ___.
why: Buddhist, with roots across the Arakan border, and their own new year water festival. Eleven recognised peoples share those three districts and outsiders routinely treat them as one, which none of them do.

q: The people of Bandarban's highest ridges, one of the smallest communities in the country, are the ___.
why: They live higher up than almost anyone else in a country that is mostly at sea level, and a religious teacher devised an entire alphabet for the language in the 1980s. The bamboo flute music is the thing outsiders usually hear of first.

q: Among the Garo of the Mymensingh hills, property and clan name pass down through the ___.
why: The youngest daughter generally inherits the house and the husband moves into his wife's family. It is one of the few matrilineal systems in South Asia, sitting a few hours' drive from a thoroughly patrilineal Dhaka.

q: The great majority of Bangladesh's Garo community are, by religion, ___.
why: Missionaries reached the hills in the 19th century and the conversion was close to complete. It is why Christmas is a visible village festival in parts of Mymensingh and Netrokona and almost invisible elsewhere.

q: The Indigenous people of the north-western plains — not the hills — are the ___.
why: Spread across Rajshahi, Naogaon and Dinajpur, farming land they have often had to fight in court to keep. Everyone pictures Indigenous Bangladesh as the Hill Tracts; a large part of it is flat, hot and grows rice.

q: The Sylhet community whose autumn Raas dance festival draws visitors from across the country is the ___.
why: They came into Sylhet from Manipur generations ago and kept the dance, the weaving and the language. The Raas is danced through the night on the full moon, and the classical Manipuri form is taught in Dhaka dance schools that have never been to Moulvibazar.

q: The Khasi villages in the hills along Sylhet's border make their living growing ___.
why: Grown up the trunks of trees rather than in fields, in settlements called punjis, and sold as Khasia paan at a premium in every market in the country. The same people live on both sides of a border drawn straight through their hills.

q: The Buddhist community of the Cox's Bazar and Patuakhali coasts, who founded Kuakata, are the ___.
why: They crossed from Arakan more than two centuries ago and settled the coast, sinking wells for fresh water — which is what gave Kuakata its name. Their weaving and their water festival are the visible part; the villages are quiet the rest of the year.

q: The Chittagong Hill Tracts are still divided among three traditional rulers known as the ___ chiefs.
why: The Chakma, Bohmong and Mong circles, each with a raja who still collects a customary tax and settles disputes. It is a colonial-era arrangement that outlived the empire that drew it and sits oddly alongside elected local government.

q: The hill farming method of clearing a slope, burning it, cropping it and moving on is called ___.
why: Dozens of crops go into one plot at once — rice, cotton, marrow, chilli, sesame — and the ground is then left for years to recover. It works when there is enough land to rotate through, and the whole argument about it is that there no longer is.

q: The staple of Hill Tracts cooking that has to be cut young or it turns to timber is ___.
why: Boiled, fermented or dried, and cooked with pork or fish paste in a way that lowland Bengali cooking simply does not do. It is the clearest line between hill food and plains food, and it is why the two cuisines share a country and very little else.

q: The pungent fermented fish paste at the base of Hill Tracts cooking is ___.
why: Related to the fish pastes of Myanmar and Thailand rather than to anything on a Dhaka table, and it announces itself from some distance. Sylhet has its own cousin of it in shidol, which divides opinion just as violently.

q: In the Hill Tracts, chicken is famously cooked stuffed inside a length of green ___.
why: Sealed with leaves and put straight on the fire, so the meat steams in the bamboo's own sap. It has since escaped into every tourist restaurant in Rangamati, which does not make the original any less good.

q: Bandarban's high crater lake, with no visible river feeding it, is ___ Lake.
why: Sitting near the top of a hill, deep, cold and unexplained, with a local story about a dragon that swallowed a village. Geologists have offered less interesting theories and have not displaced the dragon.

q: Bangladesh's Bengali-speaking Buddhist community, concentrated around Chittagong, are the ___.
why: Buddhists who speak Bengali, carry a Bengali surname and are often assumed to be from the hills, which they are not. They are usually described as the last unbroken thread back to the Buddhist Bengal of the Pala centuries.

q: The beaches north of Chittagong at Sitakunda are where the world's ___ are taken apart.
why: Vessels are run up onto the tidal flats at full speed at high water and then cut down by hand. It supplies a large share of the country's steel — most of the rebar in a Dhaka building was once a hull — and it is among the most dangerous work anywhere.

q: The hilltop Hindu pilgrimage site above Sitakunda, reached by a long stone stair, is ___.
why: One of the shakti peeth sites, drawing pilgrims from across the subcontinent for the spring festival. The climb is about two thousand steps and the view at the top takes in the Bay of Bengal.

q: The Sylheti landlord who gave away his estates and spent his life writing mystic songs was ___.
why: He began as a wealthy zamindar with a reputation for excess and ended in plain cloth, singing that the body is a borrowed house. Tagore quoted him admiringly in a lecture, which is how the rest of Bengal found out.

q: Sylhet's older name, taken from the saint buried there, is ___.
why: It turns up on cantonments, associations, restaurants and half the Sylheti organisations in Britain. The older name still is Srihatta, which is what the Sanskrit records call it and what nobody uses.

q: Sylhet's tea garden workers are largely descended from labourers brought in from ___.
why: Recruited by British planters in the 19th century on contracts they could not read, into a valley where nobody spoke their language. Generations later the community still lives inside the gardens, speaks its own mixed tongue, and is only now getting land rights.

q: Besides Sylhet and Chittagong, Bangladesh's newest tea district is the far northern ___.
why: Flat land, no colonial estates, and mostly smallholders with a few bighas each selling green leaf to a factory. It is the one part of the industry that was not built on somebody else's plantation system.

q: In Jhalokathi and Pirojpur, boats tie up in the canals to run a floating ___ market.
why: It runs for about two months a year on canals lined with guava orchards, and everything — buying, selling, weighing, arguing — happens from boat to boat. There is a floating timber market a few canals over and neither has any road access worth the name.

q: The century-old paddle steamers that carried passengers between Dhaka and Khulna were called the ___.
why: Coal-fired paddle wheelers built in Scotland before the First World War and still running well into this century, with cabin class, deck class and a dining room serving fish. The service has now essentially ended, which people are still cross about.

q: A 19th-century mystery of the southern delta — unexplained booming sounds from the sea — was named the Barisal ___.
why: Reported by surveyors and boatmen for decades: distant cannon fire with nothing to cause it. Similar sounds are logged in other deltas, and the explanations range from seismic movement to waves in the seabed — none of them settled.

q: The saying goes: paddy, river and ___ — these three are Barishal.
why: Dhan-nodi-khal, ei tine Barishal. The district is stitched together by waterways rather than roads, and a good deal of it is still reached more sensibly by boat than by bus.

q: Shrimp farming in the south-west earned its crop the nickname ___ gold.
why: It earns hard currency, which is where the name came from, and it needs salt water let into land that used to grow rice — which is where the argument came from. Whole villages have changed occupation and soil chemistry in one generation.

q: Tagore wrote a great deal of his best-known work while managing family estates at ___ in Kushtia.
why: Sent out at thirty to collect rents, he spent years on a houseboat on the Padma instead and produced the poems that would win the Nobel Prize. The kuthibari is now a museum and the river has since moved.

q: Almost all of Bangladesh's cut flowers are grown around Godkhali, in the district of ___.
why: It started with one farmer planting tuberose in the 1980s and became a trade that empties into Dhaka overnight by truck. Bangladesh gives flowers far more than it used to, and one upazila supplies almost all of them.

q: The famous cycle of folk ballads collected from the villages of ___ is known as that region's Gitika.
why: Long verse romances sung by village performers, written down in the 1920s and found to be centuries old — with heroines who choose, elope and refuse, which surprised everybody who expected otherwise. They have been translated into several European languages.

q: The great steel railway bridge thrown across the Padma in 1915, still carrying trains, is the ___ Bridge.
why: Built to carry Assam's tea and jute to Calcutta, on foundations sunk into a riverbed that shifts constantly. A century later it is still standing and the river has been persuaded, at great expense, to stay roughly where it was.

q: Dinajpur's enormous 18th-century man-made tank, dug in a famine year, is ___.
why: Dug by hand as relief work by a local raja, on a scale that is difficult to credit standing at one end of it. It is now a national park, and the fish in it are a local institution.

q: Rangamati's most photographed structure is a wooden ___ bridge across an arm of the lake.
why: It joins one hill to another across the water the Kaptai dam created, and in a high-water year it goes under and stays under for weeks. Photographs of a submerged tourist attraction are a Rangamati monsoon tradition.

q: The Hill Tracts people closest to the Chakma in language, but insistent they are a separate community, are the ___.
why: Near-identical language, different dress, and a distinct census category won after long argument. It is a useful reminder that 'Indigenous people of the Hill Tracts' is eleven answers, not one.

q: The Shiva temple that pilgrims climb to on the island of Maheshkhali is ___.
why: A temple on a hill on an island, with a Buddhist monastery and a Rakhine village on the same slope and a fair every spring that draws all of them. Not a bad summary of that coast.

q: Besides tea and paan, the Sylhet hills are the one part of Bangladesh that grows ___.
why: Small, sharp, and grown on the slopes around Moulvibazar and Sylhet town — the only meaningful citrus orchards in a country that is otherwise too flat and too hot. The crop is small and the local pride in it is not.

q: Alongside the Santal, the other large Indigenous community of Bangladesh's north-west is the ___.
why: Their language, Kurukh, is Dravidian — related to Tamil and Telugu, a thousand miles away, and spoken in villages a few hours from Rajshahi. Northern Bangladesh contains three entirely unrelated language families in about the same number of districts.

q: The village middleman who arranges a Gulf job, for a fee that takes years to repay, is the ___.
why: Land is sold or mortgaged to pay him, so the first two years abroad earn nothing at all. He is usually from the same village, which is exactly why people trust him and exactly why the debt is so hard to argue about afterwards.

q: The commonest fraud sold to Gulf-bound Bangladeshi workers is the so-called '___ visa'.
why: It is sold as a permit to work for whoever you like, which is not a thing that exists — the visa is always tied to a sponsor. Men arrive owing three years' wages to find there is no job and no legal standing.

q: Bangladeshi labour migration to the Gulf began in earnest after the 1970s ___ boom.
why: Money arrived in the Gulf faster than people did, and the building had to be done by somebody. Within a decade a country that had almost no history of labour migration had one of the largest workforces abroad in Asia.

q: Dubai's older quarter of small shops, gold souks and South Asian traders is ___.
why: Across the creek from the towers, and the part of the city that actually looks like the trading port Dubai was until fairly recently. If a Bangladeshi in Dubai says they are going into town, this is usually the town they mean.

q: On their one day off, Singapore's Bangladeshi workers fill the streets of ___.
why: Thousands of men, remittance queues out of the doors, and a pavement haircut. The city has spent years building alternatives to it and the men keep going to Little India, because that is where everybody else is.

q: Little India's round-the-clock shop, where Singapore's migrant workers buy everything, is the ___ Centre.
why: Open twenty-four hours, six floors, and stocking everything from gold chains to rice cookers to plane tickets. It is where a suitcase for home gets filled at two in the morning after a shift.

q: The country where Bangladeshi migrants make up the largest foreign community relative to its own population is ___.
why: The resorts, the construction and much of Malé's service economy run on Bangladeshi labour, in a country of a few hundred thousand people. It is the least discussed and proportionally largest Bangladeshi presence anywhere.

q: Japan's most visible export to Bangladesh is the reconditioned second-hand ___.
why: Bought at auction in Japan, shipped to Chittagong, and sold with the Japanese owner's parking sticker still in the window. A large share of the private cars on a Dhaka road began life on the other side of the continent.

q: Pilgrims returning from Hajj bring home sealed cans of ___ water.
why: Distributed in tiny quantities to a very long list of people, each of whom drinks it standing up. Airlines allow a specific ration of it per pilgrim, which is one of the few beverage rules written for a single well.

q: The prized dark date from Madinah that every Hajj returnee brings back is the ___.
why: Soft, almost black, and sold at a price that reflects the story attached to it rather than the fruit. Every other date in the box is for the neighbours; the ajwa goes to the people who matter.

q: A Bangladeshi man who has performed the Hajj is addressed forever afterwards as ___.
why: It goes on the signboard, the letterhead and eventually the gravestone, and it precedes the name for the rest of his life. In a village it is the single clearest marker that a family's Gulf years paid off.

q: The baul whose shrine at Cheuria in Kushtia draws thousands of singers every year is ___.
why: He refused to state his religion, his caste or his birth, and left several hundred songs that argue with all three. Both Hindu and Muslim claims on him are still made and his own songs are the standing refutation of each.

q: The long, slow, unaccompanied song form sung by boatmen on the big rivers is ___.
why: Sung going downstream, with the current, which is what the name means and why the phrasing is so unhurried. The melodies carry across open water for a very long way, which was the original point of them.

q: The folk song form of the northern districts, sung about cart drivers and separation, is ___.
why: The broken, catching notes are said to come from singing on the back of a jolting bullock cart. Its subject is almost always a woman waiting for a man who drives carts, or buffalo, or an elephant, for a living.

q: The song rowers sing in time with the oars at a village boat race is ___ gaan.
why: One man calls and forty answer, and the tempo is the stroke rate — the song is doing a job, not decorating one. Jari gaan is its solemn cousin, sung sitting still.

q: The travelling all-night folk theatre with painted faces and shouted dialogue is ___.
why: Performed in the round on a bare platform in a field, from dark until dawn, with no microphone worth the name and a villain who gets his own entrance music. Television and the cinema took most of its audience and it has not quite died.

q: The contest in which two singers improvise verse against each other in front of a crowd is ___.
why: Two poets, a subject thrown at them by the audience, and a rhyme scheme they have to hold while insulting each other. A rap battle by any reasonable description, several centuries older, still performed at village fairs.

q: The Baul's one-stringed instrument, plucked with a single finger, is the ___.
why: A gourd, a bamboo split, one wire, and a squeeze of the frame to bend the note. It is on stamps, posters and every tourist brochure the country prints, which is roughly what happens to a symbol.

q: The songs Tagore wrote form a genre of their own, taught and examined as ___.
why: Over two thousand of them, with the notation fixed and, for decades, legally protected against improvisation. There are schools, examinations and a lifetime of argument about whether anyone is allowed to sing them differently.

q: Tagore wrote Bangladesh's national anthem and also the national anthem of ___.
why: The only person to have written the anthems of two sovereign countries, neither of which existed when he wrote them. 'Amar Sonar Bangla' was composed in 1905, in protest at Bengal being divided.

q: Nazrul's most famous poem, and the nickname that stuck to him for life, is ___.
why: Written in one night in 1921, in a single voice that does not pause for breath, and it made him famous immediately and imprisoned him not long after. Bengali schoolchildren still recite it at a volume that alarms visitors.

q: Alongside his Islamic songs, Nazrul wrote hundreds of devotional songs to the Hindu goddess ___.
why: He named his son Krishna Mohammad, wrote hamd and naat and shyama sangeet with the same pen, and was attacked from both directions for it. It is the single most useful fact about him and the one most often left out.

q: The poet known as Polli Kobi — the poet of the village — was ___.
why: He wrote 'Nakshi Kanthar Math' as a student — a village tragedy told through the quilt a woman stitches — and it went into school syllabuses and stayed there. He collected folk songs across Bengal for years, which is why the poems sound sung rather than written.

q: The Jashore-born poet who converted to Christianity, wrote in English first, then gave Bengali blank verse, was ___.
why: He spent years trying to be an English poet, failed, came back to Bengali and rebuilt its metre from the ground up. His epic makes the villain of the Ramayana its hero, which was not a small thing to do in 1861.

q: The Rangpur-born writer who founded schools for Muslim girls and wrote 'Sultana's Dream' was ___.
why: 'Sultana's Dream' is a feminist science fiction story from 1905, written in English, in which men are kept indoors and the women run everything on solar power. She wrote it to pass the time and it is still in print worldwide.

q: Humayun Ahmed's barefoot character who walks Dhaka at night in a pocketless yellow panjabi is ___.
why: The pocketless panjabi is the whole philosophy — nowhere to keep anything, so nothing to keep. A generation of Bangladeshi teenagers had one made, and Humayun Ahmed sold books in numbers no other Bangladeshi writer has come close to.

q: Syed Waliullah's classic novel about a man who builds a living out of an invented shrine is ___.
why: The title means red cloth — the covering thrown over a grave to make it a shrine, and the entire business plan of the novel. Waliullah translated it into English himself as 'Tree Without Roots'.

q: Advaita Mallabarman's novel about the fishing communities of a dying river is 'Titash Ekti Nadir ___'.
show: Titash Ekti Nadir Naam ('A River Called Titash')
why: Written by a man from the fishing caste it describes, published after his death, and filmed in Bangladesh by Ritwik Ghatak in 1973. The river it is named for has since silted up almost exactly as the book warns.

q: 'Banalata Sen', the most quoted poem in modern Bengali, was written by ___.
why: A Barishal schoolteacher who published little, was ignored for most of his life, and is now the poet every Bengali quotes when trying to sound serious. The poem is about a face that ends a thousand years of wandering, and it is fourteen lines long.

q: The oldest surviving Bengali literature is a set of Buddhist mystic songs called the ___.
why: Found in a Nepalese royal library in 1907, written a thousand years ago in a language that Bengali, Assamese and Odia all claim as their own ancestor. The verses are deliberately obscure — the tradition calls the style twilight language.

q: The long medieval Bengali narrative poems in praise of local deities are the ___ kavya.
why: Manasa the snake goddess, Chandi, Dharma — deities of the delta rather than of the Sanskrit centre, who demand worship and get it by force in the stories. It is where the Behula and Lakhindar tale everybody knows comes from.

q: Medieval Bengali poetry's most generous patron was, unexpectedly, the court of ___.
why: Buddhist kings across the eastern border kept Bengali Muslim poets on the payroll, and Alaol wrote his best-known work there. Some of the finest Bengali of the period was produced outside Bengal entirely.

q: The verse romances read aloud to a village audience, in Bengali thick with Persian and Arabic, are ___ literature.
why: Read out in a particular sing-song by whoever in the village could read, to a room of people who could not. The mixed register it used, dobhashi, was for a long time treated as improper Bengali, which tells you a good deal about who was doing the treating.

q: Bengali's old formal literary register, abandoned during the 20th century, was called ___ bhasha.
why: Long verb forms, Sanskrit vocabulary, and a tone that made a shopping list sound like scripture. It gave way to cholito bhasha, the spoken register, and now survives mostly in old documents and in deliberate comedy.

q: Bengali letters hang from a horizontal line drawn across the top of the word, called the ___.
why: Written last, in one stroke, joining the letters into a word — which is why Bengali handwriting looks like a fence with things hanging off it. A handful of letters break the line on purpose, and children get those wrong for years.

q: Unlike Hindi, French or Arabic, Bengali grammar has no ___ at all.
why: One pronoun covers he, she and they, and no noun is masculine or feminine. Bengali speakers learning European languages find this out with some indignation, and Bengali sentences translate into English with a shrug where the gender should be.

q: Everyday Bengali words like kagoj, dokan, khobor and jomi came into the language from Persian and ___.
why: Six centuries of Persian as the language of administration left paper, shop, news and land in everybody's mouth. Bengali took vocabulary from Persian, Arabic, Portuguese, English and Turkish and declined to change its grammar for any of them.

q: Satyajit Ray's ancestral family home stands in the Bangladeshi district of ___.
why: His grandfather Upendrakishore and his father Sukumar both came from there, which makes three generations of the most influential family in Bengali children's writing and cinema a Bangladeshi one. The house at Masua still stands.

q: Sukumar Ray's book of nonsense verse, still recited by Bengali children everywhere, is ___.
why: Published the month he died, at thirty-five. Its animals are hybrids of two things that should not be joined and its logic is airtight, which is why adults quote it more often than children do.

q: The first Bangladeshi film selected at Cannes, directed by Tareque Masud, was ___.
why: A boy is sent to a madrasa by a father turning stricter, in a country about to change entirely — told almost without raising its voice. It was refused a certificate at home before it was celebrated abroad, and then celebrated at home.

q: The first full-length feature film made in what is now Bangladesh, released in 1956, was ___.
why: Made by a theatre man with borrowed equipment, no processing lab in the country, and film that had to be sent to Lahore to be developed. It is a fairly ordinary crime story and it started an entire industry.

q: Dhaka's state-built film studio complex, where most Bangladeshi cinema was physically made, is the ___.
why: Sound stages, editing rooms and a lot of parked equipment on one campus in Tejgaon, through which essentially every film in the country passed for fifty years. Digital cameras and rented flats have made it far quieter.

q: Bangladesh's commercial film industry goes by the nickname ___.
why: Tollywood already existed across the border in Tollygunge, so Dhaka needed its own. The name is used with about equal parts affection and embarrassment, which is roughly the industry's relationship with itself.

q: The biggest box-office hit in Bangladeshi cinema history, a folk romance from 1989, is ___.
why: A prince, a snake-charmer's daughter, songs every driver in the country can still sing, and takings that no film since has approached. It ran in some halls for the better part of a year.

q: International Mother Language Day began with a letter to the UN from two Bangladeshis living in ___.
why: They called themselves the Mother Language Lovers of the World, wrote to the Secretary-General, and got the idea in front of UNESCO, which adopted it in 1999. A global observance kept by dozens of countries started with a small group of immigrants in British Columbia.

q: Toronto's signposted Bangladeshi high street runs along ___ Avenue.
why: Further east than the Greek stretch everybody knows, with sari shops, sweet shops and a mela that closes the road each summer. Gerrard Street's Little India is the older South Asian strip; the Danforth is the Bangladeshi one.

q: The east Toronto apartment complex that became a Bangladeshi enclave is ___ Town.
why: A cluster of high-rises built in the 1970s where a whole community arrived building by building, because the first families told the next ones where the cheap rent was. The lifts are the noticeboard.

q: Canada admits Bangladeshi engineers and doctors who then cannot get hired for want of Canadian ___.
why: You cannot get the job without it and you cannot get it without a job. It is the single most complained-about sentence in immigrant Toronto, and it is why a driver on the 401 may well hold a doctorate.

q: Quebec picks its own immigrants, so a Bangladeshi applying to Montreal is scored on their ___.
why: Which produces Alliance Française classrooms in Dhaka full of people who have never been to France and never intend to go. It also means Montreal's Bangladeshi community grew up quite separately from Toronto's.

q: Montreal's South Asian quarter, among the most densely populated in Canada, is ___.
why: Squeezed between a railway line and a university campus, and the first address for arrivals from South Asia for fifty years. Gentrification has been eating at it from the campus end for a decade.

q: The first serious purchase of a Bangladeshi family's first Canadian winter is a proper ___.
why: Bought a size too big so it lasts two children, and photographed immediately for the relatives. Every family has the picture: three people outside a rented flat in February, smiling, visibly astonished.

q: Sydney's Bangladeshi community is concentrated in the suburb of ___.
why: Sharing a high street with a long-established Lebanese community, which makes the Ramadan night market there one of the more remarkable things in the city. The mosque, the groceries and the sweet shops are all within a few hundred metres.

q: Most Bangladeshis now in Australia originally arrived on a ___ visa.
why: A masters degree, a job, then permanent residency — an expensive route that filters hard on who can afford the first step. It has made the Australian community younger and more urban than most.

q: In Rome, Bangladeshi street sellers are famous for materialising with ___ the moment it rains.
why: Roses in the restaurants at night, sunglasses in August, umbrellas within about ninety seconds of the first drop. The logistics behind it — who watches the forecast, who holds the stock — are a genuinely impressive piece of organisation.

q: A great many Bangladeshis in Italy got their papers through a periodic government ___.
why: Italy has run several, each converting tens of thousands of undocumented workers into legal residents overnight. Whole Bangladeshi communities in Rome and the Veneto date their legal existence to a specific one, and can tell you which.

q: Barcelona's Bangladeshi community is concentrated in the old quarter of ___.
why: Narrow streets a few minutes from the Ramblas, with grocery shops, phone shops and a mosque in a converted garage. Barcelona's Bangladeshi population is one of the largest in Spain and almost invisible in the tourist account of the city.

q: Madrid's Bangladeshi and South Asian quarter is the neighbourhood of ___.
why: Wholesale clothing shops, restaurants and a large Bangladeshi association, in what was historically the poorest quarter inside the old walls. The neighbourhood's annual street festival is now half South Asian by weight.

q: Lisbon's Bangladeshi and South Asian quarter centres on the square of ___.
why: A square at the bottom of the Mouraria hill, ringed by shops and restaurants, where the number 28 tram starts. Portugal's residency rules made it one of the fastest-growing Bangladeshi communities in Europe.

q: Paris's Bangladeshi, Tamil and Pakistani quarter sits around the station of ___.
why: A few streets north of the Gare du Nord, thick with sari shops and grocers, and known to the rest of Paris as Little Jaffna after its Tamil majority. The Bangladeshi shops are woven through it and rarely get separate billing.

q: Greece's Bangladeshi migrants work overwhelmingly in ___.
why: Strawberries, olives and greenhouse vegetables, on seasonal work with very little in the way of contracts. It is one of the few European destinations where the Bangladeshi community is rural rather than urban.

q: Outside Britain, Europe's largest Bangladeshi communities are all in the ___ of the continent.
why: Italy, Spain, Portugal and Greece — the countries with the most seasonal work, the least documentation and the most amnesties. Northern Europe took Bangladeshi students and professionals; the south took everybody else.

q: Across southern Europe, the shop still open on a Sunday evening is reliably run by a ___.
why: Beer, bread, phone credit and an umbrella, at eleven at night, in a country that closes at seven. Whole Italian and Spanish neighbourhoods rely on it entirely and could not tell you which country the shopkeeper is from.

q: Bangladesh's silk weaving is concentrated almost entirely in ___.
why: Mulberry along the roadsides, a state silk board, and a product that has spent decades being undercut by cheaper imported thread. A Rajshahi silk sari is the standard gift for a wedding you are slightly too distant from to buy gold.

q: The everyday handloom cotton sari that clothes rural Bengal takes its name from the district of ___.
why: Thousands of pit looms in villages around one district, turning out saris cheap enough to wear to work and good enough to wear to a wedding. The design ownership of it has been argued over across the border more than once.

q: The coarse hand-spun, hand-woven cotton associated with the town of Comilla is ___.
why: It began as a political garment — cloth spun at home rather than bought from a mill — and became, in Comilla, a straightforward local industry. Its winter panjabis are a Dhaka middle-class uniform every December.

q: Rangpur's traditional woven floor rug, patterned in blocks of colour, is the ___.
why: Woven flat on a frame loom, historically for the floors of local households and, at one point, for export to Europe. It went into a long decline and was pulled back out of it by design work in the 1980s.

q: The smooth woven mat that stays cool to lie on, added to UNESCO's heritage list, is the ___.
why: Split from the murta cane that grows in Sylhet's wet ground, and the fine ones can be folded like cloth. The name means cool mat, which is not poetry — the surface genuinely reads cold to the skin.

q: The surname carried by Bengal's hereditary potter community is ___.
why: The same name as the Buddhist dynasty, which confuses everybody once. Their wheels also make the Durga images, so the busiest weeks of the potters' year are set by a festival calendar rather than by the demand for pots.

q: Chittagong's traditional wooden river boat, whose name English also borrowed, is the ___.
why: The word travelled the sea routes from Chinese into Malay, Portuguese, English and Bengali, and the boat with it. Chittagong's boatmen have their own song form named after it.

q: The village monsoon boat race, rowed to a drum and a called song, is ___.
why: Held when the rivers are highest, in narrow boats carrying fifty or sixty rowers, with villages backing their own like football clubs. The boats are stored under mud for the rest of the year to keep the wood from splitting.

q: The word 'rickshaw' came into Bengali and English from ___.
why: Jinrikisha — human-powered vehicle. The pulled version reached Bengal from East Asia, the cycle version arrived in Dhaka in the 1930s, and it has since become the single most recognisable object in the country.

q: Dhamrai's metalworkers cast their brass figures using the ___ process.
why: A wax model is coated in clay, the wax melted out, the metal poured into the space it leaves — so every mould is destroyed to release one object. It has been done in that town by the same families for centuries.

q: The heavy golden alloy that traditional Bengali dinner plates were beaten from is ___.
why: A high-tin bronze, hammered rather than cast, and heavy enough that a full set is a serious part of a dowry. It goes black if it is not cleaned, which is why every household has a tamarind-and-ash routine for it.

q: The long scarf worn across the shoulders with a salwar kameez is the ___.
why: Called dupatta almost everywhere else in South Asia and orna in Bangladesh, and it is doing about six jobs — modesty, decoration, sun shade, and something to grip when your mother is annoyed with you.

q: The short, collarless, everyday cotton shirt a Bangladeshi man wears at home is a ___.
why: Shorter than a panjabi, no collar, no ceremony — the difference between what you wear to Eid prayers and what you wear to buy fish. Worn with a lungi, it is the national uniform of a man who is off duty.

q: The covered chair carried on poles, in which a bride once travelled to her husband's house, is the ___.
why: Carried by four or eight bearers who sang to keep step, and used well into living memory in villages without roads. It now appears only at weddings, hired for photographs, carried about forty feet.

q: The craft retail chain that turned Bangladeshi handicraft into a middle-class purchase is ___.
why: Started by BRAC to give rural women a market for their work, and now the shop where the entire country buys a wedding present. The name means a village fair, which is a fairly generous description of a mall unit.

q: The heart-shaped hand fan plaited from palm leaf, indispensable in a power cut, is the ___.
why: Cut from a single palmyra leaf, bound at the edge, and wielded by grandmothers with a wrist action nobody younger can reproduce. Load shedding has kept an entire craft alive that electricity should have finished off.

q: The flat woven bamboo tray used to toss rice and separate out the husk is the ___.
why: The toss is a single sharp movement that throws the light husk forward and drops the grain back — impossible to learn from a description and obvious after ten minutes with somebody who can do it. It also turns up in wedding rituals, holding the things a bride is given.

q: The traditional ornament a Bengali bride wears through the septum of her nose is the ___.
why: Distinct from the nath worn through the side of the nostril, and heavy enough to need a thread up over the hair. It turns up in folk songs constantly as shorthand for a bride, and in real weddings mostly as a clip-on.

q: A married Bengali Hindu woman wears a white conch bangle and a red one called the ___.
why: Shakha from conch shell, pola from red coral, worn as a pair and put on at the wedding. The conch comes up from the far south of India and is cut in a Dhaka lane that has been doing it for four hundred years.

q: The tall white conical hat worn by a Bengali Hindu groom is made from ___.
why: The pith of a marsh plant, white, weightless, and cut into lace by craftsmen called malakar. It is worn once and generally destroyed the same evening, which is either wasteful or exactly the point.

q: Old Dhaka's Tanti Bazar was named for its weavers but is now the street of the ___.
why: Tanti means weaver, and there has not been a loom on it in living memory — the whole lane sells gold now. Half of Old Dhaka's street names describe a trade that left, which is a decent short history of the city.

q: The white rice-paste patterns painted on courtyards and floors for a festival are ___.
why: Drawn freehand with the fingers, in rice paste, on ground that will be walked over by evening. Dhaka now paints an enormous one down the middle of Manik Mia Avenue on the night before 21 February.

q: The folk art and crafts museum at Sonargaon was founded by the artist ___.
why: He founded the art school in Dhaka as well, and spent years collecting village objects nobody else thought were worth a museum. He is called Shilpacharya — teacher of art — and essentially every Bangladeshi artist since traces a line back to him.

q: The Narail painter who gave Bengali peasants enormous, heroic muscles was ___.
why: He painted farmers with the bodies of wrestlers, on the argument that the people who feed a country ought to be shown with the strength their work actually requires. He lived in Narail with a house full of children and animals and refused to move to Dhaka.

q: A nakshi kantha is held together entirely by one simple stitch: the ___ stitch.
why: The most basic stitch there is, in rows close enough to quilt several worn saris into one blanket, with the thread often pulled from the same old saris. Everything else — the figures, the borders, the story — is built out of that one movement.

q: The distinctive striped shawls and skirts woven on backstrap looms in Moulvibazar are ___ weaving.
why: Woven on a loom tensioned by the weaver's own body, so the cloth is limited to the width of the person making it. The technique came into Sylhet with the community and has become one of the few Indigenous crafts with a national market.

q: The wrapped skirt and chest cloth worn by Chakma women, woven in bands of colour, is the ___.
why: The pinon is the lower wrap and the hadi the cloth above it, and the border patterns carry information about who made them. Marma women wear the thami and Tripura women the rignai, and outsiders call all of them the same thing.

q: Bengali wooden boats are made watertight by hammering fibre and pitch into the seams — the fibre being ___.
why: The same crop that gives the country its sacking and its rope also keeps its boats afloat, which is a fairly complete summary of jute's place in the delta. The tar goes on hot, in the open, and the smell carries across a river.

q: The brightly painted earthenware pots sold at village fairs, bought for display rather than use, are ___ hari.
why: 'Hobby pots' — decorated with fish, flowers and lotus in a few flat colours, and traditionally given filled with sweets. Rajshahi's are the ones collectors want, and the painting is done by the potters' wives rather than the potters.

q: Bangladesh's most celebrated World Cup upset came in 2007, when it knocked out ___.
why: Chased down in Port of Spain by three teenagers and a captain nobody had heard of, and it sent the tournament favourites home in the first round. The celebrations at home were the kind normally reserved for a final.

q: Bangladesh's home cricket ground at Mirpur is named after ___.
why: 'The Tiger of Bengal', a title given to A.K. Fazlul Huq long before the cricket team took the animal for itself. The pitch there turns square by the third day, which visiting batting line-ups discuss at length afterwards.

q: The game in which Bangladesh produced South Asia's first grandmaster is ___.
why: Niaz Murshed took the title in 1987, before any Indian player had. Bangladesh has produced a handful of grandmasters since, on essentially no funding and a great deal of adda in Dhaka's chess clubs.

q: Dhaka football's great rivalry is between Abahani and ___.
why: In the decades before cricket took over, this fixture stopped the city — black-and-white against sky blue, with the ferry terminals and tea stalls picking sides. Older men still describe the crowds in a way the current attendance figures do not support.

q: In ready-made garments, Bangladesh is the world's largest exporter after ___.
why: From essentially nothing in 1980 to the second-largest exporter on earth, on a product with thin margins and enormous volumes. Roughly four out of every five dollars the country earns abroad comes from clothing.

q: The workforce of Bangladesh's garment industry is overwhelmingly ___.
why: Millions of them, most of the first generation of women in their families to earn and bank their own money. Whatever else is argued about the industry, that single fact reshaped marriage age, family size and village economics across the country.

q: Bangladesh's garment industry began with a training deal struck with a company from ___.
why: In 1979 a Bangladeshi firm sent a group of workers to Korea to be trained by Daewoo. Most of them left within a few years to start factories of their own, which is precisely how an industry gets seeded and precisely what the contract had not anticipated.

q: The Bangladeshi organisation routinely described as the largest NGO in the world is ___.
why: Schools, microfinance, a bank, a university, a dairy and a craft chain, operating in a dozen countries and started to resettle people after a war. Its scale is the thing outsiders cannot quite absorb: it has taught millions of children directly.

q: Grameen Bank's founding idea was to lend to the very poor without asking for any ___.
why: A group of borrowers stands behind each loan instead, which turns out to be a more reliable security than land. The interest is real and not small; it was the collateral that was the innovation.

q: The mobile money service most Bangladeshis now use to send cash across the country is ___.
why: The word also means development or blossoming, and it has become a verb — you bkash somebody money. A shop counter with a mobile and a ledger reaches villages no bank branch was ever going to.

q: Millions of tube wells sunk to end waterborne disease turned out to be delivering ___.
why: It occurs naturally in the delta's sediments and nobody tested for it, because nobody expected it. Tens of millions of wells were later painted red or green to mark which were safe, and a Bangladeshi-American chemist won an international prize for the filter that fixes it.

q: In 2002 Bangladesh became the first country in the world to ban ___.
why: Passed after blocked drains were blamed for flooding, and years ahead of anywhere else. Enforcement has been another matter entirely, which is the part usually left out when the fact is quoted abroad.

q: The engineering university whose entrance exam is the hardest in the country is ___.
why: A few thousand seats against tens of thousands of candidates, and a coaching industry built entirely around one afternoon. Its graduates are disproportionately represented in every Bangladeshi engineering diaspora on earth.

q: Bangladeshi schooling runs in three separate streams: Bangla medium, English medium and ___.
why: Three curricula, three sets of examinations and three quite different pools of graduates who go on to sit in the same offices. Very few countries run this many parallel school systems at national scale, and the consequences turn up everywhere.

q: The examination a generation of Bangladeshi graduates organises its twenties around is the ___.
why: Hundreds of thousands of applicants, several rounds over more than a year, and a coaching industry, a guidebook market and a genre of newspaper column of its own. A cadre posting is the safest job in the country and everybody's parents know it.

q: The elevated railway that opened above Dhaka's traffic in 2022 is the ___.
why: Air-conditioned, on time, and consequently regarded with a slightly disbelieving pride. It crosses in twenty minutes a distance that has been known to take two hours on the road below it.

q: The bridge that finally joined the north-west of the country to the rest of it crosses the ___.
why: Before it opened in 1998, going from Dhaka to Rangpur meant a ferry and a wait measured in hours. It is several kilometres long, carries road, rail, gas and power, and shortened half the country's journeys at once.

q: South Asia's first road tunnel under a river was dug beneath the ___.
why: Two tubes under the river at Chittagong, opened in 2023, intended to pull the city's growth onto the far bank. A country built on soft silt digging a road tunnel under a tidal river is not an obvious engineering choice.

q: Dhaka's river terminal, from which scores of launches leave every evening, is ___.
why: Three-deck launches leaving for the south at dusk, gangplanks two boards wide, and hawkers selling everything up to and including a mattress. It is the oldest way in and out of the city and still one of the busiest.

q: The great majority of Bangladesh's imports and exports pass through the port of ___.
why: One port doing the work of a national economy, on a river with a bar at its mouth that limits the size of ship able to enter. Every conversation about Bangladeshi trade eventually becomes a conversation about that channel.

q: Before the grid reached everywhere, Bangladesh ran the world's largest programme of household ___.
why: Millions of small rooftop systems sold on instalments to households a grid line was never going to reach economically. It is the most successful thing the country has done in energy and it is barely known outside the sector.

q: Typing Bengali on a computer became practical in Bangladesh with the ___ keyboard layout.
why: It solved a genuinely hard problem — Bengali's compound letters do not map onto a Latin keyboard in any obvious way — and then held the market for two decades. The free Unicode-based alternative that eventually challenged it was written by a medical student.

q: The state television channel that was for decades the only one in the country is ___.
why: One channel, one evening drama, and a country that all watched the same thing at the same time and talked about it the next day. Satellite arrived in the 1990s and that shared experience has not existed since.

q: Dhaka's diplomatic and expensive quarter, laid out around two lakes, is ___.
why: Embassies, glass towers and a supermarket where the imported cheese is priced like jewellery. Dhanmondi is older money and more books; Gulshan is newer money and more security guards.

q: The red disc on Bangladesh's flag is deliberately set off-centre so that it looks centred when the flag is ___.
why: Shifted slightly towards the mast, because a flag in the wind is seen mostly from the fly end and a centred disc would look pushed outwards. The same trick appears on a handful of other national flags and almost nobody notices it on any of them.

q: The rural market that materialises on two fixed days a week and vanishes again is the ___.
why: A bazar is there every day; a haat is an event, with its own days, its own ground and its own cattle section. Half the towns in the country have a name ending in -hat or -gunj for exactly this reason.

q: In the flood-prone north, Bangladesh runs primary schools that are literally ___.
why: Solar-powered, with a library and internet on board, collecting children from the bank and teaching while moored. It was designed for a place where the school cannot be built above the water, so it goes to the children instead.

q: The blue tin of Danish butter cookies in a diaspora kitchen is opened to reveal ___.
why: The tin outlives the biscuits by about twenty years, and every child in the house learns the disappointment exactly once.

q: The good sofa in a diaspora Bangladeshi front room spent years under a sheet of ___.
why: Bought for guests, protected from guests, and eventually thrown out still perfect. The furniture was never really for sitting on.

q: In a diaspora Bangladeshi freezer, the curry is kept in an old ___ tub.
why: No diaspora child has ever opened one and found ice cream. The label is a lie the whole household agrees to keep.

q: Under the sink in a diaspora Bangladeshi kitchen there is always a bag full of ___.
why: It is never emptied and never full, and the day somebody throws it out is the day four people need a bag.

q: A child's Eid outfit is bought a size too big so that it will still fit ___.
why: Which is how a generation of Eid photographs came to feature children with their hands lost somewhere inside their sleeves.

q: The bright red syrup stirred into milk or water at iftar tables across the diaspora is ___.
why: A rose-and-herb cordial from the 1900s that somehow became the taste of Ramadan for millions of people who could not tell you a single ingredient.

q: A British curry house menu warns you how hot a dish is by printing little ___ beside it.
why: Three is a dare and four is a decision. The scale has no standard whatsoever and varies wildly from one street to the next.

q: The committee post a diaspora Bangladeshi association argues hardest over is ___.
why: The president cuts ribbons; the general secretary controls the letterhead, the bank card and the WhatsApp group. Everybody knows which one is power.

q: In July a diaspora Bangladeshi will drive for hours and pay anything for a box of ___.
why: The box is opened on the kitchen floor, inspected fruit by fruit, and half of it is on its way to somebody else's house by evening.

q: A Bangladeshi grocery abroad is recognisable from the street by a window full of sacks of ___.
why: Nobody buys it in a bag. It is bought in a sack, carried on a shoulder, and stored in a bin that has been in the family longer than the children.

q: When a diaspora Bangladeshi community books an entire park for the day, the sport is ___.
why: The tournament runs from morning to dark, the trophy is enormous, and the catering is a car boot full of biryani.

q: The appliance a diaspora Bangladeshi family keeps out in the garage is a second ___.
why: It holds a year of fish, a wedding's worth of meat and at least one thing nobody can identify or is willing to throw away.

q: On the first day of term, a diaspora Bangladeshi child dreads the teacher attempting their ___.
why: A whole generation quietly accepted a shortened, mangled version of their own name rather than correct a register in front of thirty people.

q: The two careers a diaspora Bangladeshi parent accepts without argument are doctor and ___.
why: Both are jobs that can be explained in one word to a relative in Bangladesh over a bad phone line, which is most of the appeal.

q: A diaspora Bangladeshi extended family is held together, and driven mad, by one enormous ___ group.
why: Forty people across five time zones, nobody leaves, and every morning begins with the same good-morning flower picture from an uncle.

q: In Ramadan a diaspora mosque fills every night for the long optional night prayer called ___.
why: It is the one month of the year when a diaspora mosque runs out of parking, shoe racks and patience all at once.

q: The sign in the window of an old-school British curry house that outlasted every trend reads '___ only'.
why: The card machine has been broken since roughly 2004 and there is a cash point two doors down that everybody knows about.

q: The tray brought out with poppadoms holds mango chutney, onion salad, raita and ___ pickle.
why: Almost nobody finishes it, almost nobody sends it back, and it is doing more work than the poppadom in making the meal feel like an occasion.

q: A diaspora Bangladeshi child's birthday party is catered with a cake and an enormous tray of ___.
why: Ordered for forty when twenty are coming, because sending guests home without leftovers is a failure the host will hear about for years.

q: British Bangladeshi children learn standard Bengali at weekend school and speak ___ at home.
why: Which is why so many of them can read a textbook aloud to a teacher and still not follow a conversation between their own grandparents.

q: The one hour of the week when parking anywhere near a diaspora mosque is hopeless is ___.
why: Every neighbouring shop, side street and understanding driveway is spoken for, and the traffic warden knows the timetable better than most of the congregation.

q: Walking the length of Brick Lane, you are stopped every few metres by restaurant ___.
why: Each one will beat the last one's offer without being told what it was, which tells you roughly what the printed menu prices mean.

q: The shop a diaspora Bangladeshi family will drive right across town for is the halal ___.
why: Two miles further, ten minutes of parking, and a conversation about the mince that could have been had anywhere. That is not really what the trip is for.

q: The small cloth-wrapped amulet pinned inside a diaspora baby's clothes is a ___.
why: Handed over by a grandmother with instructions nobody writes down, and quietly re-pinned to every new outfit for about the first two years.

q: A diaspora Bangladeshi student is steered towards a university close enough to keep living ___.
why: The argument is always framed as saving rent, and it is never actually about the rent.

q: Bangladeshi tea is boiled all together in one pan, which is why a diaspora kitchen owns no ___.
why: There is usually exactly one teapot in the house, received as a wedding present, still in its box, on top of a wardrobe.

q: The pond behind a Bangladeshi village house, used for washing, fish and swimming, is the ___.
why: It is dug when the house is built, because the earth taken out of it is what the house stands on. The pond and the plinth are the same act.

q: A pond large enough to be a landmark in its own right is a ___.
why: Digging one was how a family bought a reputation. Many are older than any building near them and still carry the founder's name.

q: The narrow bamboo footbridge across a village canal, crossed with great care, is a ___.
why: Usually a single bamboo with a second one to hold, rebuilt every year after the water goes down, and crossed by children at a speed that terrifies visitors.

q: The swept earth courtyard that a cluster of Bangladeshi village houses is built around is the ___.
why: It is a kitchen, a drying floor, a playground, a wedding venue and a place to sit out a power cut, depending entirely on the hour.

q: The clay stove that a village Bangladeshi kitchen cooks everything on is the ___.
why: Built by hand out of mud, fed with rice husk, jute stick and leaves, and rebuilt whenever it cracks — which makes it furniture and appliance at once.

q: The wooden plank bed that serves as sofa, dining table and guest room is the ___.
why: No mattress, no legs to speak of, and the single most useful object in the house. Visitors are seated on it, fed on it, and eventually sleep on it.

q: The man hanging out of a Dhaka bus door shouting the destination is called the ___.
why: He collects fares, bangs the side of the bus to start and stop it, and is the only person on board who knows what the route actually is today.

q: Bangladeshis count money in thousands, then lakh, and then ___.
why: One koti is ten million, and the jump from lakh to koti is why Bangladeshi numbers so often defeat a Western spreadsheet.

q: The sound a Bangladeshi remembers the monsoon by is rain falling on a ___ roof.
why: Loud enough to end a conversation, and the reason so much Bengali writing about rain is really writing about not being able to hear anything else.

q: When the moshari is not enough, a Bangladeshi bedroom falls back on a mosquito ___.
why: Lit at dusk, balanced on a saucer, and burnt down to a grey spiral by morning. The smell is half of what a Bangladeshi summer night smells like.

q: The open market a Bangladeshi household buys its fish and vegetables at each morning is the ___ bazar.
why: Kacha means raw or unripe, so the name is really 'the raw market' — the one where nothing has been processed, packaged or decided in advance.

q: A Bangladeshi village or town neighbourhood, small enough that everyone knows everyone, is a ___.
why: It is the unit that actually organises life — cricket teams, gossip, wedding invitations and who is expected at a funeral are all decided by it.

q: The Bangladeshi household diagnosis for almost any stomach complaint is ___.
why: It explains stomach ache, chest pain, back pain, tiredness and bad mood, and the prescribed cure is always the same glass of hot water.

q: You must never tell a Bangladeshi family their baby is beautiful without also saying ___.
why: Praise without it is thought to attract the evil eye, so the compliment and the protection have to travel together or not at all.

q: The one thing no Bangladeshi household has ever been able to throw away is an empty ___.
why: It will hold spices, sugar, screws, buttons or achar within a fortnight, and everybody knows it, which is why nobody is allowed to bin one.

q: Your elder brother's wife is not called by her name — she is ___.
why: The word carries a whole relationship with it — half sister, half friend, and traditionally the one person in the house a younger sibling can joke with freely.

q: Your elder sister's husband is addressed, for the rest of his life, as ___.
why: The word has bhai — brother — built into it, which is the point: he is being told, permanently and politely, that he is now family rather than a guest.

q: In Dhaka, a stranger driving your rickshaw or serving your tea is addressed as ___.
why: It literally means mother's brother. Bengali would rather invent a family relationship on the spot than address anybody as nothing at all.

q: A Bangladeshi host hears 'no thank you' and responds by putting another piece of ___ on your plate.
why: Refusing food twice is treated as politeness rather than information, so the only way to actually stop is to leave some on the plate — which is its own crime.

q: A Bangladeshi elder conducts every single telephone call on ___.
why: Held flat, at arm's length, at full volume, in a room full of people, and there is no version of this that anybody is going to change.

q: The furniture that materialises the moment more guests arrive at a Bangladeshi house is the plastic ___.
why: Stacked on a balcony, borrowed from a neighbour, or produced from behind a wardrobe. A Bangladeshi household's real seating capacity is never what the room suggests.
